title: Government says perpetrators of financial abuse will be pursued in court
text:
Perpetrators of financial abuse who use the tax and social security systems to create debts as a form of coercive control could soon be held liable.

The federal government today announced consultation over whether courts should be given greater flexibility to transfer a tax or social security debt to the spouse responsible for financial abuse in family law proceedings.

ABC News last month flagged that Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino was taking a range of steps to combat financial abuse.

"Financial abuse is often one part of a broader pattern of coercion, control and abuse designed to remove a person's independence and limit their choices," Mr Mulino said.

Loading...

He said the effects could follow victim-survivors for years after a relationship ended, through debts, financial insecurity and lost opportunities.

"We have a responsibility to ensure our financial systems cannot be used as a tool for abuse, and that victim-survivors receive the support they need to rebuild their lives," Mr Mulino said.

The reforms form part of the federal government's response to the Parliamentary Joint Committee (PJC) inquiry into financial abuse.

Reforms to stop death benefit payouts and super rollovers

Other reforms announced include preventing perpetrators of family and domestic violence from receiving victims' superannuation death benefits, with draft legislation to be released later this year.

The government also wants to stop coerced directorships, including providing protections for victim‑survivors pressured into company directorships and associated liabilities.

Daniel Mulino says he wants to stop financial abuse through the tax and super systems. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

Mr Mulino said draft legislation would be released for consultation later this year and supported by the Australian Taxation Office (ATO).

The government would also give the ATO powers to prevent rollovers into newly established self‑managed super funds, where there are concerns of fraud, financial abuse, misconduct, or potential consumer harm.

Loading...

ASFA chief policy and advocacy officer James Koval said currently a super fund may be legally obligated to pay a member's death benefit to a person who perpetrated family and domestic violence against that member.

He welcomed moves to end it as well as stop rollovers of super in cases of abuse.

"Once money leaves the safety of larger institutional super funds and moves into a self-managed fund, it can be very difficult to recover," he said.

Financial abuse crackdown Perpetrators of domestic violence would be punished rather than rewarded for their actions when committing abuse against their former partners through the tax and super systems.

" Giving the tax office the power to stop a super withdrawal in its tracks while it investigates suspected financial abuse or crime is a sensible safeguard. "

Super Consumers Australia's director of advocacy Lily Jiang said the announcement was a positive step towards addressing the devastating impacts of financial abuse.

"We need to address the risks built into the system, identify abuse before people's savings are transferred, and make sure the professionals people rely on aren't enabling that abuse," she said.

Lily Jiang wants professionals who facilitate abuse to be held accountable. (ABC News: John Gunn)

One in six women impacted

Mr Mulino said the government would invest more than $180 million to reform the child support system and close loopholes that facilitated financial abuse and coercive behaviour, including through legislation it introduced in September.

Government proposes crackdown on economic abuse The federal government is consulting on major reforms to reduce financial abuse, including making it harder for directors to be appointed without clear consent.

It would also expand Services Australia's powers to waive social security debts incurred as a result of family and domestic violence.

Ann Kayis-Kumar, the founding director of UNSW's tax and business advisory clinic, noted one in six women and one in 13 men were impacted by "this insidious form of abuse" and hoped the law changes would soon be implemented.

She has long been calling for the ATO to waive debts in cases of financial abuse.

Ann Kayis-Kumar wants to see the ATO waive debts in cases of financial abuse. (ABC News: Scot Preston)

Lody Stewart from Redfern Legal Centre's Financial Abuse Service called for increased funding for frontline services.

"Access to specialist economic and financial abuse support remains a postcode lottery," she said.

Financial counsellor Julie Dal Pra said they supported victim-survivors who had been coerced into directorships, held liable for business debts that were not theirs, and left to spend years untangling the financial consequences of abuse.

"Coordinated action across government, industry and regulators must be backed by properly funded specialist community services and stronger accountability for perpetrators," she said.

Julie Dal Pra supports victim-survivors who have been coerced into directorships. (ABC News: Billy Draper)

The Centre for Women's Economic Safety (CWES) CEO Rebecca Glenn welcomed the reforms but called for a formal mechanism to ensure victim-survivors of financial abuse had a say in final reforms.

"Their lived experience must be central to implementation if these reforms are to achieve their intended outcomes," Ms Glenn said.

title: RACQ report finds Brisbane's petrol the most expensive of five biggest capitals
text:
Brisbane has the highest petrol prices of the five largest capital cities, with an average 199.2 cents per litre for unleaded, according to the RACQ's latest report.

That's 10.6 cents more than the previous quarter.

Meanwhile diesel prices eased slightly, from 245.6 cents per litre to an average of 242 cents per litre — but still higher than other capitals.

Simone is a South Bank local and said fuel price increases have been "ridiculous".

South Bank local Simone says the scale of the increases has been "ridiculous". (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

"I don't know how we can live like this. It's ridiculous," she said.

"They need to put it down. It's getting out of hand, it's out of control.

" I just don't know how people haven't pulled their hairs out of their heads yet. "

RACQ's price specialist Ian Jeffreys said drivers in Melbourne, Sydney, Adelaide and Perth were also paying more at the bowser, with average above 195 cents per litre for unleaded and 235 cents per litre for diesel.

"Brisbane can be more expensive because it has fewer independent stations, reducing competition", he said.

Australia could insulate against oil price shocks if we relied less on imported fuel, Dr Jeffreys said.

"Electrification and biofuel use are the quickest ways to improve fuel security, reduce our reliance on imported fossil fuels and support our economy because electricity and biofuels are already locally produced," he said.

Dr Ian Jefferys says Brisbane is more expensive because the market has less competition. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

The RACQ are calling for state governments to consider reducing dependence on imported fuel and diesel.

Dr Jeffreys said Australia is vulnerable to high prices on imported fuel.

"Electrification and biofuel use are the quickest ways to improve fuel security, reduce our reliance on imported fossil fuels and support our economy," Dr Jeffreys said.

Dylan says he think prices will stay high until global unrest eases. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

He said those products can be produced locally in Queensland.

Another Brisbane local Dylan said he was spending time shopping around for the cheapest fuel.

"The fuel price has been going crazy, I guess the war at the Strait of Hormuz is playing a part in it, and some poor decisions by the government would be playing a part as well," he said.

"Maybe the next election might change that, who knows. Until they sort out what's going on overseas I don't think it's going to come down any time soon."

title: What to know about the cancer the pope has been diagnosed with
text:
The pope is recovering in hospital after the Vatican confirmed doctors detected cancer in his lung during surgery.

Pope Leo had a lower lobe of his right lung removed on Tuesday and was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, a common form of lung cancer, the Vatican said in a medical bulletin.

Leo, 71, was admitted to Rome's Gemelli hospital on Tuesday for surgery to remove a growth on his lung that doctors found in a recent health check-up.

The pope has woken up normally and is resting in his hospital room.

Here's what to know about his diagnosis.

What is adenocarcinoma?

Adenocarcinoma is a type of cancer that starts in mucus-producing or glandular cells.

It can develop in the lungs, bowel, breast, cervix, kidney, oesophagus, pancreas, prostate and stomach.

Less commonly, it accounts for types of anal, bladder, vaginal and vulvar cancers.

Lung adenocarcinoma is often found in the outer part of the lungs.

Cancer Australia says it is the most common form of lung cancer in non-smokers and is also more likely to occur in younger people than other types of lung cancer.

What is lung cancer?

Lung cancer begins when abnormal cells grow and multiply in an uncontrolled way in the lungs.

Lung cancer can spread to the lymph nodes, pleura, brain, adrenal glands, liver and bones.

Loading...

There are two types of lung cancers: non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and small cell lung cancer (SCLC), according to the Cancer Council.

NSCLCs make up about 85 per cent of lung cancers and may be classified as adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma or large cell undifferentiated carcinoma.

Squamous cell carcinoma starts in thin, flat cells and is most often found in larger airways.

Small cell lung cancers start in the middle of the lungs and usually spread faster than NSCLC.

What is the prognosis for lung adenocarcinoma?

Lung Foundation Australia says the prognosis for lung cancer is dependent on the stage, overall health of the patient and whether genetic mutations are present.

Stage 1 has a 5-year survival rate of 68 per cent.

Early detection dramatically increases the survival rate.

The Cancer Council estimates that 15,108 people were diagnosed with lung cancer in 2025 in Australia.

The average age of diagnosis is 72.

More men than women get lung cancer but rates have steadily decreased among both genders since the 1980s due to falling smoking rates.

However, the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare said that lung cancer was estimated to be the fourth most commonly diagnosed cancer in Australia.

Among the five most common cancers in Australia, its survival rates are the lowest.

Surgeons operated on Pope Leo at Rome's Gemelli hospital. (Reuters: Stoyan Nenov)

Will the Pope's treatment be successful?

The pope's lead surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, and his personal physician, Luigi Carbone, said in a statement that the procedure lasted about 90 minutes and was successful, with no complications.

"In order to make the procedure curative, the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique," they said.

Human lungs have five lobes — three in the right lung and two in the left.

A medical expert told Reuters that to assess the pope's case, they would need to know the size of the tumour and whether the cancer had spread to his lymph nodes, information the Vatican did not immediately provide.

"While we have the diagnosis, we do not yet have the stage. This is critical to prognosis and treatment," said Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown University in Washington and division chief of hematology-oncology at MedStar Georgetown University Hospital.

"If this is a small lung cancer with no lymph nodes involved, surgery itself is likely to be curative.

"But if final analysis reveals a greater extent of cancer involvement, this indicates a poorer prognosis."

title: Conflicting advice left prospector stranded on outback tenement
text:
A prospector was left stranded on a remote tenement with dwindling supplies for almost a month due to conflicting advice from WA's former Aboriginal Affairs Minister and the state's planning and heritage bureaucracy.

Prospector Dale Richardson had approval for the tenement near Cosmo Newbery, about 1,000 kilometres north-east of Perth, since 2021 under the WA Mining Act.

But he has faced more than two years of confusion over whether he can drive out to the ground he has pegged without breaching WA's Aboriginal Heritage and Planning laws.

Dale Richardson says the experience has been confusing. (Supplied: Dale Richardson)

In a move WA's peak mining and exploration body says highlights the need for reform of the laws, the confusion culminated in Mr Richardson being stranded on the tenement, unsure if he could leave without breaching the law.

He was on the tenement on February 27 this year when he received advice from the Department of Planning, Lands and Heritage that he could no longer drive along the remote White Cliffs-Yarmarna Road, contradicting previous advice he had obtained.

He stayed until his supplies ran low, leaving on March 21, but left his caravan and most of his prospecting equipment behind.

In September, Mr Richardson was told by the department that he had breached Section 31 of act by using the road, but no formal action would be taken against him.

Years of confusion

The road at the heart of Mr Richardson's situation passes through the Cosmo Newbery West and South Aboriginal Reserves, generally requiring permission to access under the Aboriginal Affairs Planning Authority Act.

But in December 2024, former Aboriginal Affairs Minister Tony Buti wrote to Mr Richardson confirming he did not need a permit to travel along the road.

That advice was reversed in February, when the department advised the minister's earlier ruling had been incorrect, based on an additional investigation and information provided by Central Desert Native Title Services.

The department initially advised the road Mr Richardson was using did not meet the gazetted route, and he would be obliged to use a track that had not been maintained for more than 60 years.

Dale Richardson says this is the track Don Punch said he had to use to access his tenements. (Supplied: Dale Richardson)

But in a subsequent update, it ruled a Federal Native Title decision meant the road was no longer gazetted, and he would need a separate mining permit to use it.

A Department of Planning, Lands and Heritage spokesperson said advice on road access had been based on the information available when access to the tenements was initially sought.

"I've done everything that I was legally supposed to do," Mr Richardson said.

"I've tried to get a permit, I've tried to negotiate an agreement, they're just not willing to do so for some reason."

The Yilka Talintji Aboriginal Corporation, which represents the area's native title holders, declined to speak to the ABC.

White Cliffs-Yamarna road, at the start of Cosmo Newberry Reserve. (Supplied: Dale Richardson)

Limited government response

While not at risk of prosecution, Mr Richardson said he had been left with little opportunity to retrieve his caravan and equipment.

Aboriginal Affairs Minister Don Punch intervened late last week, granting the prospector a three-month permit to return to the site, remove his property and secure his prospecting equipment.

The limited permission does not allow Mr Richardson to resume prospecting.

Don Punch granted Mr Richardson a three-month permit to access the site and secure his equipment. (ABC News: Briana Shepherd)

Labelling the matter complex and unusual, Mr Punch said the Aboriginal Lands Trust had only wished to grant Mr Richardson seven days' access, but he had opted to overrule the body.

"Since being made aware of the matter, my office has remained engaged with the relevant parties," he said.

Mr Richardson said he wanted to work and rehabilitate his tenements, actions he continues to hold a license for.

"Minister Punch has taken the easy way out, instead of addressing the issue he has only allowed me to collect my belongings and vacate," he said.

Association of Mining and Exploration Companies (AMEC) chief executive Warren Pearce said the prospector's situation highlighted the need for clearer rules around land access and exploration.

Warren Pearce says heritage and access rules need to be better understood. (ABC News: Phil Hemingway)

"There is a strong case for targeted amendments to the relevant act to provide greater certainty for all parties, while ensuring Aboriginal cultural heritage continues to be appropriately protected," he said.

"The Glen Kelly Review identified opportunities to improve the way native title and cultural heritage processes operate in Western Australia.

"The subsequent committee established must deliver meaningful improvements that reduce confusion and unnecessary barriers to exploration."

title: Live: Short's Pies move off as Dons consider deadline day pivot to Cats star
text:
Eagles fan - I am sure our list managers know what they're doing but I'd personally take Viney and Rivers for pick 23. We are going get an end of first round compo pick to basically replace that pick anyway after the bids happen. - Dan

First of all, judging by the comments in this blog over the past two weeks I'm not sure all Eagles fans mirror your faith in the list management at the club.

It is a good point that West Coast is set to get pick 24 back from the AFL after a bid is placed on Dougie Cochrane on draft night. It's also true that West Coast are pretty tight for list spots this year.

Do they just bite the bullet and do the deal for 23, take picks 3 and 24 into the draft and then maybe save a late one for a potential bid on Harper Banfield? Or do they really try to protect this all-important draft hand before Tassie arrive next year? We also know they've been trying to get another pick inside the first 15, though I'm not sure how that happens now.

A lot for Matt Clarke and co to ponder.

title: Failed caravan company AOR allegedly traded insolvent since 2023
text:
A failed Queensland caravan manufacturer may have been trading while insolvent for three years, according to administrators, who say the company owes $14 million.

Australian Off Road (AOR) shut its doors in September after 26 years operating on the Sunshine Coast, becoming the second local van manufacturer after Zone RV to collapse within a year.

Nearly 50 customers face losing $2.25 million after making progress payments toward caravans that were not built.

They include Sandra Muller from NSW Southern Highlands, who stands to lose $101,000.

Sandra Muller has paid $101,000 towards her caravan, which was not built. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

In a report to creditors on Tuesday night, administrators DVT McLeods detailed fresh allegations against directors Russell Evans and Steve Budden and said AOR may have been insolvent for more than three years.

Potential offences identified included insolvent trading, reckless or intentional dishonesty, failure to act in good faith, and improper use of position to gain advantage.

"We have a preliminary view that the company traded whilst insolvent from at least 30 June 2023," the report stated.

Administrators also said AOR's creditor bill had grown to $14 million, up from $9 million estimated last month.

The administrators said further investigations were required and that the results would be reported to ASIC, the corporate regulator.

The ABC has attempted to contact Mr Evans and Mr Budden.

Director plots buyout

Mr Evans is one of two parties offering to purchase the company out of administration.

He has pitched to investors seeking $2 million to resurrect AOR in a move that could leave existing customers empty-handed.

It is legal for a director to buy and transfer a company's assets into a new business if the sale is approved by creditors.

The ABC has seen an email from Mr Evans outlining his vision "to establish a new, financially disciplined premium off-road caravan manufacturing business".

His proposal offered 20 cents in the dollar for the company's assets, while the existing company's debts would not carry across.

The pitch pledged to "recognise customers who paid deposits" and "investigate practical solutions for affected customers" but did not clarify whether all progress payments would be honoured.

Inside the Australian Off Road factory in China. (Supplied)

Mr Evans said the new business would have "a clean financial structure" and "a clear pathway to sustainable profitability and growth".

Mr Evans's proposal detailed projected annual revenue of $11.3 million with production of 84 caravans, or seven a month.

The new venture would "create a new, low-cost and scalable caravan business", he wrote.

Despite marketing itself as an Australian manufacturer and blaming imported Chinese vans for its demise, the ABC can reveal AOR was making chassis in China.

A separate company with a factory north of Shanghai was established in 2025 to reduce AOR's production costs.

The Chinese company is owed $518,000 but falls among the unsecured creditors.

Allegations detailed

AOR made a loss in three of the past four financial years, and had a negative asset position of $3 million when it collapsed, the creditors report stated.

Administrators engaged Argus Auctions to advertise the sale of the business or its assets.

After receiving 200 enquiries, 20 parties signed non-disclosure agreements, with feedback that "stock was outdated and poorly managed" and there was a "lack of operational systems and structure".

Russell Evans joined AOR about 2012 and became a director in 2021. (Supplied)

Only two parties made offers to buy the company, including Mr Evans's proposal.

The administrators said they were investigating allegations that caravans fully paid for by some customers had been delivered to other people.

The report noted the company's CCTV system ceased recording on September 9, the day the company stopped trading.

"Due to the limited clarity and quality of the footage … we are unable to determine with certainty … whether any caravans were moved within or removed from the premises," the report stated.

The administrators said they were "yet to receive a substantive response" from Mr Evans about the claims.

The report shows Mr Evans is claiming $67,000 in unpaid leave, while Mr Budden and his wife, Rhonda, are each owed $22,000 in holiday pay.

Steve Budden founded Australian Off Road from his garage in 2000. (Supplied)

AOR is owed $165,000 by two companies and a trust related to the directors, and the administrators have issued letters of demand to repay the outstanding money.

The administrators recommended creditors vote to delay the next meeting to allow time to sell the business.

"If the company was placed into liquidation, it is unlikely that there would be a distribution to the unsecured creditors [including customers]," the report said.

Administrators are claiming $283,000 for their services, more than 10 times their initial estimate.

title: Afghan batter recreates infamous hamstring injury used against Australia
text:
Sediqullah Atal's maiden Test century has led Afghanistan to an epic draw against Bangladesh in a one-off cricket Test.

Afghanistan batted for 142 overs, 92 on the fifth and final day, in its second innings to force a sensational draw on Tuesday. It began the day on a dodgy 132-3, lost five more wickets, but fought on to hold out to stumps at 346-8.

But it was the actions of number nine Qais Ahmad in the dying minutes that drew the most attention in the match's final act.

With the finish line in sight and just two wickets left, Ahmad played a forward defence to spinner Taijul Islam before collapsing to the ground clutching his hamstring.

The Bangladesh team was not impressed, and had commentator Ahmad Farhad Fidai in stitches as he likened it to the actions of Afghanistan's Gulbadin Naib, who suffered a suspicious cramp fielding at slip in their famous 2024 T20 World Cup win over Australia.

"Qais Ahmad does it again. This reminds me of Gulbadin Naib," an amused Fidai said, clearly believing Ahmad's fall to the turf was nothing more than time-wasting antics.

"Oh boy, not again.

"You really don't need to see the replay; we can understand from here what's going on."

Ahmad soldiered on and finished the match with a six over midwicket.

Bangladesh dominated the match after winning the toss and batting first. Bangladesh earned a first-innings lead of 106 runs, then declared its second innings at 7-372 after player-of-the-match Litton Das was out for 102. That gave Bangladesh an imposing lead of 478 and four and a half sessions to bowl out Afghanistan.

But Afghanistan defied the odds despite losing two wickets in the first seven overs on Monday.

First drop Atal, in his third Test, ate up most of the chase as he faced 332 balls over 8.5 hours to score 111. He was caught close to the wicket after tea, the seventh man out.

Afghanistan still had 23 overs with just tailenders left. But 34-year-old Yamin Ahmadzai faced 85 balls for a career-best 19, and Ahmad, who has played franchise cricket in eight countries, faced 80 to finish with an unbeaten career-best 49.

AP/ABC

title: Reassessment of billion-dollar silver mine sparks tractor protest
text:
Plans for a $1 billion silver and lead mine in Central West New South Wales are being reassessed as opponents take to the streets of Mudgee in tractors to protest.

Approval of the Bowdens Silver Mines Limited project was deemed "void" by the NSW Court of Appeal in August 2024.

It had been approved by the state's Independent Planning Commission (IPC) in April the previous year.

That decision was overturned when the court ruled the IPC should have examined the potential environmental impacts of the project's transmission line.

The IPC has now started three days of hearings as part of its reassessment.

Silver Mines Limited managing director Jo Batershill told the panel today the merits of the project were now stronger than when it was approved in 2023.

He said it was in the best interests of the local and regional economy, the state's strategic minerals goals and the nation's contribution to the global renewable energy transition.

"The strategic rationale is now stronger today that when it was originally approved," Mr Batershill said.

The proponents are seeking approval to extract 30 million tonnes of ore over 23 years.

A group of protesters gathered in Mudgee ahead of the public hearing on the Bowdens silver project. (ABC Central West: Hamish Cole)

Tractor protest

Today's "tractorcade" was similar to a protest held in 2023 when residents of Lue, about 26 kilometres east of Mudgee, disrupted traffic through the famous wine region.

Protester Tom Combes, who farms sheep and cattle at Lue, described the mine proposal as "just nuts".

Tom Combes was one of more than 40 residents outside the IPC hearing in Mudgee with signs and shirts voicing their opposition to the development. (ABC Central West: Hamish Cole)

"All the people that live out there, all of their lifestyle, their health and their amenity is going to be destroyed," he said.

" We're not going to have a bar of it. "

Mr Combes is one of 97 speakers set to give evidence over the next three days.

Lead concerns

A conditional safeguard measure introduced by the IPC during the previous assessment saw Silver Mines Limited offer voluntary blood testing for residents and, in particular children at Lue Public School, 2 kilometres from the project.

Janet Walk lives 9 kilometres from the proposed site and told the IPC the offer made her nervous.

"You don't test children's blood unless you think the lead is going to appear in the blood," she said.

"There is no safe level of lead in a child's blood.

"The monitoring will tell us that the child has lead in their blood, but it won't stop it, it won't treat it."

Janet Walk told the hearing that the mine could put children at risk. (ABC Central West: Hamish Cole)

Tractor protest participant Jamie Inglis, whose cattle property is 5 kilometres from the site, shared that fear.

"There are a number of concerns… contamination of Lawson Creek, which is the lifeblood of our farmers," he said.

"We don't need silver and we definitely don't need lead."

Susannah White raised about the potential impact of lead on livestock. (ABC Central West: Hamish Cole)

Susannah White was worried about the future of her beef farm on Lawson Creek, downstream of the proposed mine site.

She referenced the Australian and New Zealand Food Standards Code, which stipulates that livestock cannot be sold or consumed if lead above 0.24µmol/L is detected in the animal.

"If this mine is approved it means our business is unviable," she told the hearing.

"These animals could need destroying because they can't be sold and they can't be moved.

"What are the animal welfare implications when you run out of feed because you can't sell the animals like you normally would?"

The initial approval

The 2023 IPC decision was successfully challenged by the Bingman Catchment Landcare Group.

The court found the panel failed to consider the impacts of a 13km transmission line that the Department of Planning and Environment had deemed required a separate application.

Dozens of people drove tractors from Lue to Mudgee, where the IPC is holding a three-day hearing into the Bowdens silver mine application. (ABC Central West: Hamish Cole)

In response, the state government passed legislative changes that allow off-site infrastructure for state significant projects to be assessed separately.

With the original project approval still considered void, the project must now be reassessed.

Fresh assessment

A new three-person panel of commissioners was appointed in September to make a new determination on Bowdens's proposal, with the IPC stating the "previous determination has no influence on this new assessment".

No changes have been made to the original project application, but Silver Mines Limited has provided additional advice to the state's planning department that will be considered.

The proponents of the Bowdens silver mine are seeking approval to extract 30 million tonnes of ore over 23 years. (ABC Central West: Mollie Gorman)

Mr Battershill told the panel that additional assessments, including biodiversity and climate change reports, showed "the merits of the project before the commission today remain unchanged".

While admitting that the project was not supported by everyone in the community, Mr Battershill pointed to a supplementary report provided by the Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure that found the "project benefits outweigh its residual costs and that the project is in the public interest and is approvable".

The IPC initially scheduled two days for the hearing but added a third following significant community interest in the development.

It is expected to make a determination by December 9.

title: Less can be more for Rugby League World Cup
text:
The only things that stay the same about the Rugby League World Cup are that it never stops changing and it continually has to justify its own existence.

For the third tournament in a row, there will be a different format and a different number of teams, dropping from 16 to 10, and for the umpteenth tournament in a row, the sceptics will question why it's worth playing a Rugby League World Cup at all and compare it unfavourably to the rugby and football versions.

Those world cups exist in different universes than the league equivalent, even as nation-swapping and diaspora-heavy squads, two hallmarks of the much-maligned international rugby league, become more prevalent in their larger cousins.

The Rugby League World Cup has to prove itself anew every four years. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

Measure the Rugby League World Cup against those that dwarf it in scale and it will always be miles behind. It is playing a different game, one that is carving out a place all its own.

On the back of the rise of Tonga and Samoa over the past 10 years, Test football is at its strongest and most vibrant in years, with the two Pasifika nations emerging as legitimate draws and top-class teams.

Tonga's two matches against Australia in the 2024 Pacific Championships drew crowds of more than 33,000 and 28,000, and both Tonga and Samoa have made their first tours to England since the last World Cup.

When the ancient island rivals went head-to-head in Brisbane last year, more than 40,000 came through the gates, the second-largest non-World Cup final crowd for a Test in Australia in the last half-century.

Samoa creates rugby league magic The passion of the Pacific shines through in Samoa's rugby league team, and the pride the people have is evident on the island.

A similar attendance is expected for the tournament opener between Australia and New Zealand on Thursday night, and if the Sydney Football Stadium can sell out, it'll be the biggest Test crowd in Sydney since 1974.

It marks the beginning of a chance for the Rugby League World Cup to reshape itself a little more permanently and take advantage of the renewed interest by recasting itself as a pinnacle for the game rather than a starting point.

Rugby league had to make a choice whether its World Cup was a beginning or an end, a proving ground for developing nations or a battleground for the best, because it could not be both at the same time.

At the sharp end of recent tournaments, when it's the best teams in the world having it out, the product is reliably compelling, rich and powerful. The problem is it's just taken too long to get there.

In 2022, there was a crackerjack knockout phase, highlighted by Samoa's epic win over Tonga in Warrington, New Zealand sneaking home against Fiji in Hull, and two brilliant semifinals, including a golden point epic that doubles as one of the best games in the tournament's history.

The night a rag-tag group of rugby league Russians took on the world champions Russia might only make one trip to the Rugby League World Cup but the memories forged in the 2000 tournament, especially in their record loss to Australia, are wild enough to last a lifetime.

But the group stage was a forgone conclusion almost all the way. Only two of the 24 preliminary matches were decided by one score or less. There were 10 scores over 60 and two scores over 90.

Australia's 110-4 massacre of Russia in 2000 remained untouched as the most lopsided result in World Cup history, but matches from 2022 fill out the second, third and fourth spots on that list.

Developing nations have their place in the international rugby league and the emotional scenes upon qualification for Jamaica, or Greece's epic tale of playing qualifying matches on the edge of war zones and in undisclosed locations to stay one step ahead of the authorities, are proof of the value developing nations can bring.

But it is hard to see the benefits of England nearly putting 100 points on the Greeks, or a disinterested Australia beating Scotland 84-0.

The trickle-down effects of those games, such as they are, can take decades to rise to the surface, if they ever do at all.

The knockout phase of recent World Cups have been rugby league dynamite. (Getty Images: Gareth Copley)

The game's wholehearted embrace of the set restart rule and the increased speed of play makes it harder for the smaller nations to compete on a physical level, and the perfunctory nature of the group stages makes the tournament even longer.

In a world where fan interest and player fatigue are already being stretched to their limits, it adds even more to an already overstuffed season.

So while it may not please the true believers, the move to 10 teams is a good one. This tournament is leaner and has the potential to be meaner.

The lack of northern hemisphere teams — it's just England, France and Lebanon, with none from the Americas and no other home nations after Scotland and Ireland were demoted to affiliate status and Wales failed to qualify — is regrettable, but exclusivity cuts both ways because less can be more.

This is a tournament with barely any fat on it, and as a result, it's as open at the top as it's ever been.

Australia is still the favourite because such is the largesse of talent available that it's almost impossible to name a Kangaroos team that isn't oozing with class, but it's far from invulnerable.

Its talent pool has been diluted, and there are several squad members who are coming off indifferent or underdone seasons.

Some have made it due to coach Kevin Walters's loyalty to the side that retained the Ashes in a 3-0 whitewash last year, but others are in because there's a lack of other options as the eligibility rules slowly spread the talent around.

Nobody has benefited more from that spread than New Zealand, who welcome Kalyn Ponga to the squad for his belated Test debut as the herald of a new era.

On paper, it's a better side than the one that handed Australia its biggest-ever defeat just three years ago — it has all three middles from this season's Dally M Team of the Year — and a second World Cup title is a distinct possibility.

The bookies have Samoa and Tonga as equal-third favourites to make the final, well ahead of England, and their group-stage clash at Parramatta Stadium has been sold out for months.

Samoa and Tonga have already sold out their group stage match. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

The English have a little more to prove after last year's lacklustre Ashes showing, an embrace of heritage players that has divided their fan base and the controversial exclusion of Leeds halfback Jake Connor from the squad.

Outside the top five, there's still plenty to follow. Write off the perennially underrated Fijians, who beat New Zealand in 2017 and came within six points of doing the same in 2022, off at your peril.

France and Lebanon won't be as dangerous, but the French have 20 homegrown players in their squad and 10 of Lebanon's starting 13 for their first game have NRL experience.

Even the Cook Islands, which will play in front of crowds that dwarf its home's population, will have Cronulla's KL Iro and former Kangaroo Valentine Holmes to call upon.

Another Australian victory is far from a guarantee in this World Cup. (Jan Kruger: Getty Images for RLWC)

Injuries have robbed Papua New Guinea of some of their biggest names, but their group matches against Samoa and Lebanon will be the Kumuls' biggest on home soil since the PNG Chiefs were admitted to the NRL and shape as the first dress rehearsals for what awaits the game in the land where they love it most.

Through it all, this World Cup can have it all. There will still be stories of paupers taking on princes against all odds and of the unbridled passion and pride that has kept international football alive despite the many obstacles.

Those tales and teams will always have their place, but for the most part, this tournament will be collections of top-level rugby league talent crashing into each other in the fast until only the world champions are left to rise from the wreckage.

What the tournament gives up in diversity and novelty, it can win back in quality, because at some point, a World Cup has to be about the best of the best being at their best, and there are more nations who can dream of that than ever before.

Never in the World Cup's 72-year history has the sky seemed so open. Ten teams might not seem like many, but if five have designs on the crown, it can be plenty.

title: Finance presenter Alan Kohler to sign off from ABC for final time
text:
Where to start? Let's try the beginning.

A kid, straight out of school with no real future mapped out, no obvious talents, just a general inclination that he might be suited to journalism.

"The reason I wanted to be a journalist is because English was the only subject in high school I was any good at," he said.

" I basically failed everything else, didn't get into university, so I had to get a job. "

It doesn't sound like an auspicious start.

No grand ambitions to rise to the top of Australian journalism, to edit several of the nation's most prestigious and influential newspapers and to become the doyen of business and economics reporting.

Alan Kohler is ending an ABC career spanning more than three decades. (Supplied)

Alan Kohler will walk out the door of the ABC's Melbourne studios tonight after presenting his final finance report, ending a 31-year career at the public broadcaster, 24 of them as the business big kahuna.

"I love the ABC and I do really like going to the studio, but I think it's time to not have to do that," he confessed on the ABC's Business Daily podcast.

"I'm 74."

Life as a hippie

Kohler's media career was well established long before he joined the ABC in 1995.

After a brief period as a copy boy for The Australian in 1969, making coffee and organising dry cleaning, he was hired as a cadet.

After completing a cadetship, Alan Kohler fell into finance reporting. (Supplied)

His pathway into the heady world of business and finance, however, was entirely accidental.

"A job came up at the Oz and it happened to be in the finance section," he explained to Jonathan Green a decade ago.

"That was it."

He was just as directionless after completing the cadetship.

Hitching to Darwin, he scored a job on the NT News, was caught up in Cyclone Tracy's devastating rampage across the city and helped put together emergency issues of the paper on a "borrowed" printing press on A4 stapled paper.

Alan Kohler was a member of the team producing an emergency edition of NT News in the aftermath of Cyclone Tracy. (Supplied: Alan Kohler)

It took another four years, after wandering around the country, before he became serious about life and work, transforming from "being a pothead, to discovering ambition".

He scored a job at The Age, met his future wife, journalist and author Deborah Forster, and set off for Europe where he worked on regional English papers before returning to Melbourne and The Age.

Alan Kohler travelled in Europe in the 1970s. (Supplied)

By 1979, he'd switched to the Australian Financial Review under the tutelage of Robert Gottliebsen, rapidly ascending to penning its premier column, Chanticleer.

Business reporting had found him, rather than the other way round.

As he explains, it's partly because very few want to do it, and so the pay is better. Plus, he realised he had a talent for explaining things.

"People's brains just go to toothpaste when it comes to finance," he told the Daily Business podcast's Carrington Clarke.

Loading...

But the old inertia played a part too.

"Once you get in a particular role, it's hard to get out of it," he told Green.

But the coasting days were long gone. He taught himself economics, reading until late into the night, put his mind to the intricacies of finance and delved into the daily machinations of the corporate world.

By the time he was 32, he was editor of the AFR, during the heady days of the Hawke and Keating government as deregulation swept the world and Australia opened its doors to the global economy.

Alan Kohler, left, with then Treasurer Paul Keating in 1984, during his time as editor of the Australian Financial Review. (Supplied)

A chance encounter

Our paths first crossed in 1986.

It was the decade of greed, takeover fever was in full swing and a then-corporate raider, the since-disgraced Ron Brierley, had launched a massive bid for miner North Broken Hill.

It coincided with a journalist strike at metropolitan newspapers.

As AFR editor, and with no staff on hand, Kohler went back on the tools to write the analysis piece and opted for wire copy from Australian Associated Press for the news story.

I was that AAP author and thrilled to be given a byline on the paper's page one lead story. But it was his work that was instructive.

Rather than the complex, almost unintelligible explainers routinely trotted out by the AFR's senior reporters, Kohler's analysis was simple, illuminating and elegant.

Kohler on the stories he missed In his final column, Alan Kohler reflects on the stories that shaped him and Australia in ways he could not predict.

It was a masterclass in communication and forever seared into your correspondent's memory.

Two decades later and he joined the Sydney Morning Herald during my tenure as business editor. In 2012, I joined his operation, The Eureka Report, for a year.

And for the past 13 years we've worked alongside one another at the national broadcaster.

A new chapter?

He may be stepping down from the ABC, but Alan Kohler is not retiring.

Journalism is moving away from organised newsrooms, he argues, and more towards individuals delivering their own content.

In his case, he will be moving away from the ABC at Southbank and more towards working from home.

Alan Kohler is optimistic about the future of journalism. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

While free-to-air networks and newspapers still have a role to play, streaming, mobile devices, video and audio on demand and the loss of advertising revenue for the major players have transformed the media industry in the past 20 years.

These pressures show no signs of abating and traditional media is likely to continue to feel the squeeze, both in broadcast and in text.

And then there's artificial intelligence.

"I'm actually starting to feel optimistic about what we do now because with AI, the work that humans do will be more valuable," Kohler said.

"How that plays out, I'm not quite sure. I mean, I think a lot of grunt work of journalism will be done by AI, but I do think that consumers of media will value human work."

Despite the ongoing changes and challenges, Kohler is adamant that if that same kid from the late 60s was transported to the present and scouting around for a career today, he'd still pick journalism.

"Absolutely. It's been a wonderful career," he said.

"It's been so good to me, I couldn't wish for anything better."

title: 'Stranded patients' in NSW hospitals prompts call for change
text:
New South Wales must think outside the box to stop the number of "stranded" aged care patients in hospitals from spiralling out of control, the state's productivity commissioner says.

According to recent data from NSW Health, the number of people who occupied hospital beds while awaiting placement in aged care facilities had jumped almost 40 per cent over the past year, from 761 to 1,063 patients.

A new report from the NSW Productivity and Equality Commission, released on Wednesday, estimated that figure could reach more than 7,000 in 10 years if aged care and community care services failed to keep pace with Australia's ageing population.

The report, which was commissioned by the state government, said an extra 2,600 aged care beds would be needed each year to meet future demand, but NSW was projected to deliver only 660.

It said the costs associated with patients stranded in NSW hospital beds were estimated to exceed $1 billion annually.

Patients waiting for aged care beds in hospitals has risen by 40 per cent in a year. (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

NSW Productivity and Equality Commissioner Peter Achterstraat told the ABC more funding was required for aged care support and health prevention, but other alternatives could be explored.

"We need to look outside the box. There may as well be a third alternative, such as intermediate care where people can go to facilities which are not an acute hospital but not quite an aged care facility," he said.

Peter Achterstraat emphasised the need for intermediate care. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

Mr Achterstraat said previous research conducted by the commission found that keeping patients in hospital beds was costing $1,000 a night, compared with "just a few hundred dollars" at an aged care facility.

"If an elderly person is at home and they have an accident or something and they need to go to the hospital … normally they'd be ready after five days to go home," he said.

"But in many situations they can't go home because they need someone at home to change the bandages or to administer medicines.

"So they stay in hospital, they can't go home and there's no aged care facilities available for them because there's a shortage … there are over 1,100 people in New South Wales hospital beds today who shouldn't be there."

NSW government responds

Ryan Park says the state government will provide interim support services. (ABC)

NSW Health Minister Ryan Park said the state government would provide interim services, but argued aged care was traditionally the responsibility of the Commonwealth.

In early September, state and territory leaders called for the Commonwealth to expand its Support at Home package to help stranded patients return home sooner.

The productivity commission is also calling for the service to be expanded, estimating there were more than 100,000 Australians waiting to access funding for at-home support services in March 2026, with average waits of about 12 months.

Mr Park said the state government would introduce a $28 million pilot program, which could include funding for short-term services such as clinical care, wound care and symptom management, personal care, as well as domestic assistance.

"It is a significant reform because we're essentially stepping into a space [that is] traditionally the responsibility of the Commonwealth, but I can't see hospital beds continue to be taken offline each and every day," he said.

Funding not in line with building new aged care homes

The commission's report found Commonwealth government funding for new aged care homes had not kept up with rising construction and operating costs.

It said the federal government was not providing sufficient returns to recover the up-front costs of new homes; the biggest barrier to increasing supply.

Bed block costs $3m per day in Queensland It didn't take long for 80-year-old Gwen to lose her ability to walk.

"Meaningful and sustained reductions in stranded patients will require the Australian Government to ensure the capacity of aged care services keeps pace with population needs," the report said. "The Australian Government should increase residential aged care funding to efficient levels that support development feasibility, long-term investment confidence and the supply response needed as the population ages."

The office of federal Aged Care and Seniors Minister Sam Rae said the Commonwealth worked with states and territories "in good faith".

"It is now time for them to deliver on their promises to give Australians better access to health services, when and where they need them," a government spokesperson said.

"The Albanese Labor Government secured a record $25 billion hospital funding deal with state and territory governments to help cut waiting lists, reduce waiting times in emergency rooms, get older long stay patients out of hospitals and manage ramping.

"Under the record funding deal, the Commonwealth is delivering an additional $6.5 billion to New South Wales, taking the Commonwealth contribution to New South Wales to $64 billion, over five years."

The spokesperson said by the end of the decade, their spending on aged care services would be "more than $50 billion each year".

Other recommendations include establishing a dashboard to track stranded patients in NSW hospitals, ensure aged care funding supports demand, expanding community based services, as well as setting up a cross-agency delivery team to coordinate action on aged care supply and stranded patients.

title: Storms 'swirling like a tornado' leave trail of destruction in parts of NT
text:
Central Australian businesses and residents are assessing damage from severe, tornado-like storms that swept through parts of the Northern Territory.

Rain, hail and winds at speeds of nearly 100km/h hit the outback town on Monday afternoon, ripping roofs from houses, knocking down trees and powerlines and covering roads with leaf litter and mud.

The Double Tree Hilton suffered significant damage. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

Double Tree Hotel general manager Todd Grierson said multiple parts of the Alice Springs building were extensively damaged after footage circulated online of rain blowing in under the front doors and water pouring through the ceiling above the reception desks.

"There is just so much more throughout the building … from our tenancies, to our beauty salon, other restaurants, our ballroom and meeting areas and back of house too," he said.

"But thankfully, the way any direction of this storm has hit us, hasn't had any effect on our guest rooms."

Cleaning up at the Double Tree Hilton. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

Mr Grierson estimated the repairs would cost more than half a million dollars to complete.

Alice Springs cafe The Roastery threw out thousands of dollars worth of food after widespread power outages.

Owner Kim Hopper said the cafe received a delivery on the day of the first storm, but food safety rules meant they had to discard many products.

Kim Hopper says thousands of dollars worth of food was discarded. (ABC Alice Springs: Mitchell Abram)

"Our staff are there at the moment just documenting it all and tipping hundreds of litres of milk down the sink," she said.

"It'd be thousands to replace that cost, but it's a loss of the sales as well … we'll be doing an insurance claim on that, and luckily we've got that in place."

'Unbelievable' storm widespread

About 20 kilometres east of Alice Springs, Undoolya Station copped a lashing, with owner Ben Hayes saying the storm was devastating.

"It was swirling, it was like a tornado. It didn't know where it wanted to go, it was just coming every direction. I've never been in a storm like that before in my life," he said.

"It was unbelievable lightning. I don't know what the hell's been hit around here, whether any of these trees have been hit, but a lot of them are screwed up."

Ben Hayes in front of his historic storeroom. (ABC Alice Springs: Charles Geary)

Mr Hayes said there had been significant damage to infrastructure on the cattle station, including a lean-to collapsed onto a house, smashed windows, a chook pen blown away and the roof of a historic storeroom ripped off by wind.

"There's a lot of history in this room and [my wife] Nicole's rattling it all out, drying it out, trying to save as much as we can," he said.

"We've got a few shipping containers up the dump with a lot of these records left to go in there, until we can find somebody to help put a roof on this thing for us."

The storeroom contains historic documents, which have been relocated to a storage container for safe keeping. (ABC Alice Springs: Charles Geary)

Meanwhile, cattle stations near the Northern Territory – South Australian border were battered with large hailstones.

Lyndavale Station, 250 kilometres south-west of Alice Springs, recorded hailstones the size of golf balls.

An eight-year-old girl’s death was preventable, a coroner has found as she criticised a Melbourne emergency department doctor’s response. Amrita Varshini Lanka’s parents nodded and wiped away tears as Victoria’s deputy state coroner Paresa Spanos handed down her findings on Wednesday. Chandra Sekhar Lanka and Satya Tarapureddi arrive at an inquest into the death of their daughter Amrita Lanka. AAP Amrita died from lymphocytic myocarditis, or inflammation of the heart muscle, at Monash Children’s Hospital on April 30, 2022. She had presented at the emergency department about 1pm on April 29, following two days of stomach pain, nausea and vomiting.

Related Article Coroners Court of Victoria Hospital ignored repeated pleas for help before eight-year-old’s death, court told Testing quickly ruled out appendicitis, so hospital staff began working on the basis she had gastroenteritis. Early the next morning, Amrita’s mother Satya Tarapureddi raised concerns with staff that her daughter was experiencing chest pain and a shortness of breath. Amrita underwent an electrocardiogram (ECG) half an hour later at 3.30am, which came back abnormal and led the emergency department registrar Patrick Tan to suspect she had myocarditis. He consulted with another colleague, who agreed with his preliminary diagnosis.

Advertisement

But neither doctor seemed to appreciate the severity of Amrita’s condition, the coroner said. Amrita’s blood pressure was not measured at that time, but other testing showed elevated lactate, which signified that she was deteriorating. Amrita Lanka died in hospital aged eight. Justin McManus Despite this, Dr Tan determined that Amrita did not look unwell. He did not attend to the eight-year-old again until 5.30am, when it was clear her condition had worsened. Her care was escalated to senior clinicians and specialist units, but she suffered a brief cardiac arrest at 7.30am.

Advertisement

Staff then organised emergency transfer to the Royal Children’s Hospital and a crew arrived about 8.51am, by which time Amrita had gone into prolonged cardiac arrest. Despite efforts at CPR, she could not be saved. In a 2024 inquest into Amrita’s death, Monash Health admitted staff had failed to appreciate the seriousness of the girl’s condition. Amrita’s family says that if tests had been interpreted correctly sooner, her case would have been escalated to an on-call cardiologist. Justin McManus On Wednesday, Spanos determined Amrita’s death was preventable. “When the ECG had been completed and the elevated lactate was available [at about 4am], Amrita’s life could have been saved,” the coroner said in her findings.

Advertisement

“While I accept that [emergency departments] are busy places and Dr Tan was a relatively junior doctor with many responsibilities, the clinical management and care he provided to Amrita was wanting,” the coroner said. His actions, Spanos told the court, “thereby caused or contributed to her death”. The coroner did not make any formal recommendations, instead commending Monash Health for undertaking an internal review following Amrita’s death. Spanos acknowledged the hospital had implemented a series of changes as a result, including requiring emergency department clinicians to notify on-call consultants in specific cases. The coroner, who at times appeared to hold back tears while reading her findings, offered her condolences to Amrita’s parents seated in the courtroom.

Moonlight Resources has put some serious numbers on the table at its Clermont gold project in central Queensland, defining a significant new exploration target of up to 662,000 ounces of near-surface gold. The study has prompted the company to launch a 13,000-metre reverse circulation (RC) drilling program to test its ambitious new objective. The exploration target covers three key prospects – Leo Grande, Goldfinger and Petersens. It ranges between 16.2 and 19.8 million tonnes at grades of between 0.94 and 1.15 grams per tonne (g/t) gold, totalling 443,000 to 662,000 ounces of the yellow metal. The company has emphasised that the exploration target is conceptual in nature and at this stage, requires more work to determine whether a gold resource can be identified and quantified in potentially economic terms. Moonlight Resources’ phase two reverse circulation drilling underway at its Leo Grande prospect, part of the company’s Clermont Project in Central Queensland. The lion’s share of the target relates to the central Leo Grande prospect, which contributes between 281,000 and 420,000 ounces of gold. The Goldfinger and Petersens prospects add some higher-grade spice, with the southern Goldfinger prospect tipped to potentially contain between 95,000 and 142,000 ounces at a solid 1.2 to 1.5g/t gold. The more northerly Petersons prospect offers the remaining potential - 67,000 to 100,000 ounces of gold at 1g/t to 1.22g/t. Moonlight’s 13,000m RC drilling campaign is now underway, with the drill bit already probing Goldfinger’s potential. The program will drill an estimated 5000m into the prospect, with a further 4000m allocated to Petersens and Leo Grande.

Advertisement

‘We believe Clermont can develop into a significant gold project.’ Moonlight Resources managing director Greg Starr The Clermont project is centred 15 kilometres west of the historic Clermont township, in a hotspot with a strong history of gold mining, producing roughly 400,000 ounces since 1878. The greater region is richly endowed and hosts several multi-million-ounce gold deposits, providing a compelling case for the region’s prospectivity. Two notable nearby projects within the Drummond Basin - the extensive regional-scale geological complex that hosts Moonlight’s Clermont ground - include GBM Resources’ one-million-ounce Twin Hills gold resource north of Clermont and its 330,000-ounce Mount Coolon gold project northwest of Emerald and north of Clermont. The Drummond Basin overall is a premier gold province credited with a total historical production and known endowment of up to 7.5 million ounces of gold. Moonlight’s exploration model rests on a solid foundation of historical work combined with its own recent successes. Earlier drilling by the company of an estimated 15,000m at Leo Grande returned a swag of broad, near-surface gold hits, including a notable 42m at 1.01g/t gold from surface and 40m at 1.31g/t gold from 76m. Moonlight Resources managing director Greg Starr said: “This Exploration Target puts some significant numbers around exactly what excites us about Clermont – the combination of potential scale, gold mineralisation relatively close to surface and the opportunity to test extensions that remain open. We’ve brought together the historical and recent drilling information at Leo Grande, Goldfinger and Petersens, which gives us a much clearer picture of the potential opportunity and where we intend to focus our efforts.”

While gold is Moonlight’s primary focus, its Clermont tenure also hosts the Peak Downs copper prospect, a few kilometres south of Clermont, which the company describes as a “high-grade copper sleeper opportunity”. This is hardly surprising, given that the prospect was historically mined between 1862 and 1877, reportedly producing around 100,000 tonnes of ore at an eye-watering average grade estimated at 17 per cent copper. Management is targeting near-term delivery of a maiden gold resource estimate for the Clermont gold project, which will initially incorporate its Leo Grande and Goldfinger deposits. Moonlight also says that it expects to deliver a much-anticipated initial copper resource estimate for the Peak Downs project before the end of the year. Test cricket great Steve Waugh is calling on Australia’s selectors to stop “messing around” and “pick and stick” at the top of the batting order. That includes keeping first Test hero Matt Renshaw, who made 190 and 82 in Durban to set up Australia’s 214-run win in the three-match series, in the middle order. Matt Renshaw celebrates his fighting century. Getty Images “They need a consistent line-up,” Waugh said. After suffering an embarrassing nine-wicket loss to Bangladesh in August to kick-start Australia’s marathon 12 months of cricket, Pat Cummins’ men continued their resurgence on Tuesday by taking down the world Test champions in Durban.

Advertisement

The outstanding victory came despite some day one wobbles, where the visitors slumped to 6-124 before Renshaw batted superbly with the tail to register his second Test century – and first in almost a decade – to set up the win. The 30-year-old faced 397 deliveries during his 190. Despite several teammates getting starts in the second innings, including Nic Maddinson (48), Marnus Labuschagne (37) and Beau Webster (39 not out), the big Queenslander was again the only Australian to pass 50. Loading Following the Test, Cummins said Australia’s brains trust, including coach Andrew McDonald and selectors, would continue to be flexible with the top seven. That included the possibility of Renshaw moving up to the top of the order and either Travis Head or Maddinson sliding down to No.5. “We’re always big on how the order functions as a whole,” Cummins said. “Seeing the way that he played spin in the one-day series led me to the thought [that] he would look pretty good at No.5.

Advertisement

“Give us a few days, we’ll look at the conditions of the next Test and whether that’s still the case. I mean, it’s got to be pretty compelling to move him from there. But we’ve seen Travis Head down at No.5 as well — [he] can do a job.” Cummins added: “I think bringing Maddo in, we really like the idea of bringing that flexibility. That unlocks a lot – Trav back to No.5, Renners down at No.5, even Maddo himself at No.5. We haven’t had that option the last few years where we feel like we’ve got plenty of options at the top. You know we’re very big on that flexibility.” Matt Renshaw and Pat Cummins celebrate on day five in Durban. AP But Waugh said the time for tinkering was over, especially given there were crunch series – five Tests in India and an Ashes in England – in the next 12 months. “We’ve been messing around with the top order for the last couple of years and it hasn’t worked, so they’ve got to pick and stick now,” he said.

Advertisement

Having earned the reputation as Australia’s “Ice Man” during his illustrious career, Waugh said he was particularly impressed by Renshaw’s application in Durban. “It was an outstanding win,” Waugh said. “And great to see some old-fashioned Test match batting from Renshaw. I think he led the way – the old values of shot selection and patience and determination – and it was great to see some Test match batting like that. It was fantastic. “I think the other guys will follow the way he batted. I think it’s a great role model for not only our team, but for world cricket – how to be successful in Test matches.” Asked whether Renshaw should stay in the middle order – where Waugh made his name during a 168-Test career that produced 10,927 runs at an average of 51.06 – the former captain said he would not change a winning formula. “It’s obviously a career-defining moment for him and could be the catalyst for great things going forward,” Waugh said. “Don’t mess around with that now. He’s been successful, and he’s comfortable, so I’d keep him there for sure.” As for Maddinson, whose 38-ball 48 got Australia off to a flyer in the second innings following his painful 33-ball first-innings duck, Waugh admitted it was a “left-field selection” to recall the 34-year-old, but hoped he continued to build a case for selection. “I wanted to see him get runs. He’s in the team now. Let’s hope he can get some runs,” Waugh said. The second Test starts on Sunday at St George’s Park, Gqeberha.

And the All Blacks were only too happy to provide inspiration as their rugby league counterparts prepared to take on the tournament favourites. “Really good, really cool,” Kiwis coach Stacey Jones said of the support of the All Blacks. Kiwis players pose for a photo with members of the New Zealand All Blacks on Thursday. AAP “I know that our boys were watching their game on the weekend, and a lot of their players enjoy watching rugby league. So it’s great that there’s a connection.” There once was a time when the rival codes wouldn’t be seen together. And despite the Warriors making inroads in All Blacks-mad New Zealand, union is still the preeminent code for the nation.

Advertisement

However, the chance to conspire against arch rivals Australia was too good to refuse. “Very special,” Jones said. “Cross-code now is a lot closer than what it used to be. Obviously, [we are] getting ideas from what they do, and if they get some stuff from us, then brilliant. But yeah, it’s just got to benefit both codes … Kiwis coach Stacey Jones. Getty Images “It’d be pretty special [for both New Zealand teams to win], particularly while some of these All Black boys are down to support us, and we’ll obviously be supporting them. So, it’d be huge for all Kiwis, especially those that are on this side of the Tasman.” Kiwis captain James Fisher-Harris, who was involved in a jersey presentation with his All Blacks counterparts, said their presence was a timely boost.

Advertisement

“It’s pretty cool, hey?” Fisher-Harris said. “Obviously, the ABs and some of the boys, obviously the other code, but it’s just all love and supporting each other. I think there’s a couple of them coming tomorrow to watch the game, and hopefully we can go watch their game on Saturday, too, so it’s pretty special.” Asked if they had been inspired by the All Blacks’ win over the Wallabies last weekend, the Warriors prop said: “Not just that test, but just in general – how dominant and how they go about their business and represent New Zealand. [There] are lot of things that they do that we look up to, so, yeah, it’s pretty cool.” James Fisher-Harris warms up. Getty Images Much of the build-up to the World Cup opener has focused on the strength of the New Zealand pack. In Naufahu Whyte, Moses Leota, Joseph Tapine and Fisher-Harris, Jones has at his disposal a pack that – at least on paper – is one of the strongest assembled. “We have the potential to be the best,” Fisher-Harris said when asked if the pack is the best he has played with.

Advertisement

The Australians go into this campaign without Payne Haas and Lindsay Collins, but coach Kevin Walters said his pack shouldn’t be underestimated. “It’s a strong New Zealand side, certainly, but I feel like the guys that we have picked in the Australian squad, they’re not mugs,” Walters said. “We’ve got Origin players, Test players, premiership winners, so that side of it – that’s what the World Cup is all about – seeing the best players on the world stage. Fortunately, from Australia’s point of view, we provide a lot of those players.” Walters opted for Reece Walsh at fullback and Mitchell Moses at halfback for the opening game, but said James Tedesco and Sam Walker will get their chance in game two.

Advertisement

“Everyone will play next week who’s not playing this week,” Walters said. “I feel that’s my objective as the coach is to give everyone an opportunity. “I could happily play all of them tomorrow, but we’ve only got 19 positions in the side for tomorrow’s game, but that will change next week.”

PLC Resources has taken to the skies, metaphorically speaking, to launch a two-stage satellite geo-spectral survey across its Abbotts gold project in Western Australia’s Murchison region, to pinpoint alteration zones and structures, sharpening the gold target discovery process. The company says its survey will cover all four of its Abbotts tenements spanning 205 square kilometres and will sift through PLC’s ground for large mineral alteration and undetected structures that can be tell-tale signs of orogenic gold mineralisation. Hyperspectral imagery over PLC Resources’ Abbotts gold project in WA will be harnessed to define structural gold targets for maiden discovery. The first stage involves a regional screening using hyperspectral EnMAP imagery by remote-sensing specialists Geo Spectra. Multispectral data will then map the alteration geological structures in greater detail across the entire project and over an additional 300 square kilometres of surrounding ground. The second, higher-resolution stage will allow Geo Spectra to zoom in on priority areas with imagery as sharp as 31 centimetres, mapping telltale iron oxides, clays and sulphates to refine targets for a boots-on-the-ground follow-up.

Advertisement

‘Hyperspectral and high-resolution satellite data can help map alteration minerals and fine-scale structures.’ PLC Resources executive director Simon Phillips The satellite survey builds on PLC’s recent high-resolution airborne magnetic survey, which revealed a large-scale fold structure considered highly prospective for gold deposition. Management says the structure is a crustal-level feature that extends for more than 14km of strike and, importantly, continues south into ground held by recent WA discovery dynamo New Murchison Gold. New Murchison has been making waves in the region, successfully trucking its high-grade gold discoveries to nearby toll-treating facilities, providing a compelling real-world example of the Abbotts greenstone’s unloved potential. PLC Resources executive director Simon Phillips said: “This survey gives us a project-wide view of Abbotts that we can’t get from the ground alone. Hyperspectral and high-resolution satellite data can help map alteration minerals and fine-scale structures that may be associated with gold mineralisation, across all four of our tenements at once.” The company’s move comes as exploration activity continues to ramp up across the white-hot Murchison, with nearby explorers committing to significant exploration programs in hopes of becoming the next New Murchison Gold story - recently capped at $950 million.

Advertisement

King River Resources recently launched a massive 11,000-metre drilling campaign at its Mindoolah gold project, while new players such as Parbo Resources, Golden Dragon and Reach Resources have all expanded their footprint in the region. The company recently completed a follow-up reverse circulation drilling program at its Rochefort gold prospect within Abbotts, with assay results currently pending. Geological logging from that campaign confirmed the target host rock had been intersected, with multiple accounts of potential gold-bearing sulphide alterations. The real test, however, will come when the assays land, potentially revealing a virgin gold discovery. PLC says, beyond drilling a Rochefort, it expects a prioritised target map from the new satellite survey within four to six weeks. The results will be integrated with recent magnetic survey data to rank targets for follow-up field exploration and aircore drilling. With New Murchison recently stacking up multiple high-grade discoveries next door along what appears to be a highly prospective, unloved gold belt, the company has plenty of reason to feel ambitious about its unfolding gold story at Abbotts. Its high-tech targeting could fast-track the hunt for a discovery of its own, with the coming months shaping up as a potentially pivotal period for the Perth-based explorer. NSW Premier Chris Minns has emerged victorious in a stoush over a controversial Central West gold mine after the Federal Court threw out a ban made by then-environment minister Tanya Plibersek, who stalled the mine on Indigenous heritage grounds. Federal Court Justice James Stellios on Wednesday decided to send the $1.3 billion McPhillamys mine proposal back to the current minister Murray Watt, determining Plibersek’s original decision lacked procedural fairness. The proposed McPhillamys gold mine would process as much as 8.5 million tonnes of ore a year. Nick Moir The decision did not make any judgment about the merits of any claims of Indigenous heritage in the area, but found Plibersek’s decision-making was flawed. That declaration prevented Regis Resources from building a tailings dam to store byproducts from mining operations at the headwaters of the Belubula River, after an Indigenous group argued the area was significant to a Dreaming story about the blue banded bee. The mining company argued that made the project unfeasible.

Advertisement

The declaration also triggered unrest between the state and federal governments, with Premier Chris Minns insisting the mine must go ahead. The state government had originally approved the project. Related Article Climate policy ‘Triply nervous’: Massive coal mine braced for challenge after High Court ruling “I want that mine to go ahead, I understand that that’s not the view of the federal government, but we need the investment,” Minns said before the judgment on Wednesday. “There are more people in mining jobs in NSW today than there were when we were elected in March of 2023. We’re proud of that.” When asked if the then-environment minister had made the wrong call when she made the order blocking the mine, Minns replied: “Yes”.

Advertisement

Plibersek’s statement of reasons for the declaration said she “could not be assured that the NSW legislative framework as it currently stands can adequately protect the specified area”. Watt said in a statement the federal government respects the court’s decision and is getting advice on next steps. He said the court’s findings highlighted the complexities of the current cultural heritage processes. “First Nations people, industry and state and territory governments have been clear with us for some time that they feel the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Heritage Protection (ATSIHP) Act doesn’t give enough certainty. We remain committed to working alongside them on a better system,” he said. NSW Resources Minister Courtney Houssos said the mine had already gone through a “robust” planning process and said critical minerals projects were important to diversify the state’s economy. “Protecting Aboriginal cultural heritage and progressing key mining projects should not be a zero-sum proposition,” she said.

Advertisement

After making the declaration in 2024, Plibersek rejected suggestions from Regis Resources that the ban killed the project, insisting the mine could still go ahead if the dam was moved. The company said finding a new site for approval would take up to 10 years, but the state government flagged it would fast-track the project. The application to protect the dam area was made by Wiradjuri-Gamillaroi woman Nyree Reynolds on behalf of the Wiradyuri Traditional Owners Central West Aboriginal Corporation. Minns told a budget estimates hearing in 2024 that the local Aboriginal Land Council had been consulted as part of the original approval process. In a statement to the ASX from Regis Resources CEO Jim Beyer after the judgment, Beyer said the company would actively participate in any redetermination of the Indigenous heritage claim by the current minister. “After considerable delay and uncertainty, and more than two years of time lost, we are eager to move forward. We look forward to engaging constructively with the Department through the redetermination process, and to advance one of Australia’s largest undeveloped gold projects – one with the potential to deliver lasting economic and social benefits to the Central NSW region and our broader stakeholder community,” he said. title: A second Eurovision contest is approaching. Here's how Australians can watch
text:
IN BRIEF: The first-ever Eurovision Asia will come to Australian screens in November.

Meanwhile, applications to represent Australia in Eurovision 2027 will open soon.

Australians will be treated to a second instalment of Eurovision this year, as the competition's first Asia series will broadcast from Bangkok in November.

On 14 November, 11 countries will take to the stage in Thailand's capital for the grand final of the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia.

Eurovision Asia's first competitors revealed

The contest will feature artists representing Bangladesh, Bhutan, Cambodia, Laos, Malaysia, Mongolia, Nepal, the Philippines, the Republic of Korea, Thailand, and Vietnam, and will be broadcast live on SBS.

Multi-hyphenate entertainer and global icon Courtney Act will steer the show, returning as SBS' Eurovision commentator.
