More than 3.27 million Australians tuned in to Eurovision on SBS this year, where Courtney Act and special guest commentator Danny Estrin guided audiences through the spectacle of the world's biggest music entertainment event.

Eurovision Asia will be no exception, with Thai television personalities Woody Milintachinda, known for hosting the talk shows Woody Talk and Woody Kerd Ma Kui and model, actress, TV host and activist Cindy Bishop hosting the inaugural event.

A decade-long journey to the stage

The project has been in the making for a decade, with the original proposal for an Asia-Pacific iteration of the popular song contest driven by SBS.

The first edition was initially planned for 2017, but the project faced repeated delays before SBS stepped away in 2021, citing difficulties with the COVID-19 pandemic.

You don't have to be Delta Goodrem to have what it takes, with SBS saying it is searching for "distinctive, contemporary songs ready to connect with people on one of the world’s biggest music stages".

Artists are invited to register their interest in representing Australia, and songwriters to submit an original song for consideration via the SBS Song Portal for Eurovision 2027.

Eligible songs must run for no longer than three minutes, include at least one Australian citizen in the songwriting team, and not have been released or publicly performed, in whole or in part, before 1 September.

Australia's 2027 entry will be selected through an internal SBS process, and submitting a song or registering interest through the portal does not guarantee selection.

Further details will be available on the SBS Song Portal from 17 October until 7 November.

title: Matildas thrash Haiti as World Cup preparations continue
text:
In brief The Matildas have defeated Haiti in an international friendly match.

Midfielder Leticia McKenna delivered a powerful performance, scoring two goals.

The Matildas bounced back from a defeat to Germany with a commanding 7-1 win over Haiti as they continue preparing for the FIFA Women's World Cup.

Matildas midfielder Leticia McKenna boosted her chances of selection for her first FIFA Women's World Cup after scoring twice.

Fresh off a humbling 4-2 defeat to powerhouse Germany, and without Arsenal star Steph Catley, Australia got their World Cup preparations back on track in Chambly, France on Wednesday.

McKenna was the spark, as she produced two classy first-half strikes before an own goal by Haiti defender Kethna Louis.

Goals to Caitlin Foord, Daniela Galic, Clare Wheeler and Holly McNamara completed the victory.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The Nottingham Forest midfielder has now secured three goals in four national team appearances, adding a selection headache for coach Joe Montemurro.

When the Matildas mentor was asked if he thought his team was ready for next year's World Cup, he laughed and said "no".

"We need time ... It's probably more about selecting the squad because now we're starting to build a big roster of players, and I need more time to make a decision on who I can bring," Montemurro said.

"It was a good window for us. We played against Germany ... We felt that we were not far, and we know the areas where we need to fix."

READ MORE Two goals but no win for Matildas in Germany friendly

Along with McKenna, the Australians midfield produced a masterclass as Alana Murphy dispatched a crafty pass to set up Galic while Wheeler had an assist and goal.

"I was a spectator in 2023, and I loved watching the group. It only made me hungrier to want to be a part of it," McKenna said.

"So to be in a position to potentially be selected is amazing."

Matildas dominate in second half

Questions had loomed over captain and star striker Sam Kerr's fitness after she complained of ankle soreness following the German clash, but she was also influential, playing a big role in two of the goals.

The rousing victory helped the Matildas firmly keep their No.15 world ranking, which currently puts them in pot two out of four for the World Cup draw, meaning a mathematically better chance for a more favourable draw.

It wasn't a smooth-sailing win for Montemurro's players though, as their first-half defence looked timid when their Caribbean opponents employed their counterattack, but they utterly dominated the second half as Haiti's wheels fell off.

It took just 80 seconds for the Matildas to draw first blood when Wheeler cut the ball back to McKenna, who produced a sublime one-touch strike into the roof of the net.

But moments later, Haitian midfield star Melchie Dumornay tucked the ball into the bottom right corner to equalise.

On the stroke of halftime, McKenna re-established the Australians' lead when she pounced on a loose ball in the box and buried it in the bottom left corner.

In the 53rd minute, Foord poked the ball to Kerr, who steered it goalwards and found the foot of Louis.

The sparkling Foord-Kerr combination wreaked havoc again when the Arsenal winger scored before substitute Galic found her first international goal.

Wheeler added her name to the scoresheet when her cross bound for Foord snuck into the bottom left corner before McNamara iced the game.

title: 'Voice for peace': Albanese sends Pope Leo well wishes after cancer diagnosis

In brief Pope Leo had a lower lobe of his lung removed in a surgery and has been diagnosed with lung cancer.

The surgery was successful with no complications, according to the Vatican.

Pope Leo had a lower lobe of his right lung removed during surgery and was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, a common form of lung cancer, the Vatican said in a medical bulletin.

Leo, 71, was admitted to Rome's Gemelli hospital on Tuesday for surgery to remove a growth on his lung that doctors found in a recent health checkup.

Tuesday's surgery lasted about 90 minutes and was successful with no complications, the Vatican said. The pope has woken up normally and is resting in his hospital room.

The Vatican said previously that the pope was expected to spend a week in hospital recovering.

"We hope and pray for a quick recovery."

The surgery marked the pope's first hospitalisation since he became head of the Catholic Church on 8 May 2025. Chicago-born Leo, the first US pope, is sporty and was believed to generally be in good health.

In a surprise announcement following Angelus prayers on Sunday, Leo told crowds in Rome's St Peter's Square that doctors had discovered the nodule "at a very early stage" during medical checks.

"The doctors believe it would be right to intervene," he said.

The Vatican has historically been very secretive about the health of popes, but began to be more transparent during the illness of Leo's predecessor Francis, an Argentine who freely discussed his ailments.

Ahead of the surgery, the Vatican said the pope's recovery time was expected to be about a week. His audiences have been cancelled until 20 October.

He is scheduled to travel to South America from 6 to 17 November to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.

It's not immediately clear what will happen if the pope requires a longer treatment or recovery.

Under church law, a figure known as the Cardinal Camerlengo — or chamberlain — takes over administrative duties if the pope dies, but pontiffs do not have a deputy to replace them if they become incapacitated.

title: She was once engaged to Donald Trump Jr. Now the White House wants her to resign
text:
In brief The Trump administration has asked Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign as US ambassador to Greece.

The former Fox News host has been embroiled in corruption allegations. She denies wrongdoing.

United States President Donald Trump's administration has asked his ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign, the White House said, amid allegations that she sought money from a Trump supporter and accepted lavish hospitality from wealthy Greek businessmen.

"We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign," Trump's new press secretary Katie Zacharia told reporters at her first White House briefing.

The announcement came a day after Trump acknowledged that he was considering dismissing Guilfoyle, a former Fox News host and ex-fiancée of his eldest son, Donald Trump Jr.

"She was doing a good job, but we didn't like what we were reading," Trump told reporters after the announcement, adding that he had not spoken to her, but that "she will not be there".

In a statement on X, Guilfoyle appeared to confirm she would leave her post. She rejected the allegations against her and defended her record as ambassador, highlighting efforts to boost US energy exports and strengthen security ties with Greece.

"These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity," she wrote.

Guilfoyle thanked Trump and secretary of state Marco Rubio, pledging her continued loyalty to the president.

"While my time as Ambassador may be coming to an end, my commitment to President Trump, the America First movement, and the country I love will never end," she wrote.

Guilfoyle has faced mounting scrutiny following a series of reports by The Wall Street Journal about her financial dealings and relationships with wealthy businessmen.

The newspaper reported that she asked Eric Deters, an influential Trump supporter, to pay off $100,000 in personal credit card debt shortly before her Senate confirmation hearing in July 2025.

Guilfoyle, a former Fox News host, served as an adviser to Donald Trump's 2024 presidential campaign. Source: Getty / Bloomberg

"Honey please I need you to get this done for me today," she wrote to Deters in a message accompanied by instructions for paying her credit card company, according to the Journal, which published screenshots of the exchanges.

Deters refused to make the payment, telling the newspaper that doing so would have cost him his marriage.

Guilfoyle's lawyer has disputed the authenticity of the messages and denied wrongdoing.

Who is Kimberly Guilfoyle?

Guilfoyle, a prominent figure in Trump's Make America Great Again movement, was appointed ambassador after her relationship to Donald Trump Jr. ended quietly in 2024. They got engaged in 2020.

She played a prominent role in her father-in-law's political circles, including as an adviser to his 2024 presidential campaign.

A former prosecutor, she was married to California's Democratic governor Gavin Newsom between 2001 and 2005, before going on to work at Fox News.

She stayed in Trump's orbit following her split from his son, with the president announcing in December 2024 that he would nominate her to serve as ambassador to Greece.

She was confirmed by the Senate in September last year and sworn in the following month.

Ethics allegations

The Journal also reported that Guilfoyle boasted of luxury trips and hotel stays funded by wealthy Greek businessmen, citing hundreds of messages, emails and other records, including recorded conversations.

She travelled to the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, aboard a private jet with Alexandros Exarchou, chief executive of Greek construction company Aktor Group, according to the newspaper.

The State Department's inspector general is investigating whether Guilfoyle received improper gifts, according to US media reports.

title: The Australian housing challenge not being solved
text:
In brief Millions of spare bedrooms sit empty as downsizing stalls.

The costs of moving may be reshaping Australia's housing crunch.

Australia's rapidly growing older population has more wealth than ever and millions of spare bedrooms, yet financial incentives are pulling many away from downsizing, new research suggests.

Almost nine in ten older households (aged over 55) have at least one spare bedroom, and 60 per cent have two or more, twice the rate of households aged 25 to 54, new research published in the GemLife Downsizing Australia Report found.

The most popular homes among the 2,100 buyers over 50 looking to downsize surveyed were two and three-bedroom properties, offering low-maintenance living, good security, and proximity to amenities. But separate research indicates there is not enough of this housing being built.

There are about 13 million empty bedrooms across the country, but older people rely on spare rooms for grandchildren, visiting family, home offices or hobby rooms, Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute (AHURI) Managing Director Tom Alves told SBS News.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

He said their research has found 60 per cent of homeowners aged between 65 and 74 in 2001 were living in the same property 15 years later. And among those aged over 75, fewer than 15 per cent downsized.

AHURI has called for developer incentives to build medium-density housing designed for ageing.

People over 55 are projected to surge from the smallest group until 2028 to the largest in 2069. Credit: Australian Bureau of Statistics

Independent Kooyong MP Monique Ryan told SBS News that making better use of existing housing is one of the few short-term levers that can address the housing crisis.

"Downsizing can help younger families get into larger homes, unlock capital for older Australians, and limits urban sprawl," Ryan said.

Reasons to stay

The family home is a primary store of wealth for many older households, so releasing its equity can mean a loss of the age pension or other benefits, and more retirees are now carrying mortgage debt, Alves said.

"Other financial barriers to downsizing include upfront costs such as stamp duty incurred when purchasing a new home and agent fees incurred during the sales process," Alves said.

"Older households are also unlikely to be eligible for a traditional mortgage, which can create a blockage to moving."

Reasons to go

Changing the age pension assets test and building new senior housing within federally funded developments would help, Ryan said.

"Most important though is that the federal government should support the states in phasing in the replacement of stamp duty with a broad-based land tax, as has been suggested by the Productivity Commission and a number of other Treasury and Senate inquiries."

Stamp duty policy has shifted in South Australia, with exemptions for seniors purchasing some new homes, while concessions also exist in Victoria and the ACT.

A family home is generally exempt from the age pension assets test, but money unlocked through the sale of a house can become taxable if it is not used to purchase another principal home.

From January 2023, money from a home sale intended to buy a replacement can be exempt from an assets test for up to two years, with a conditional one-year extension. But any surplus profit can be taxed.

The federal government also lowered the age from 65 to 55 for downsizers to put up to $600,000 from their home sale into superannuation in January 2023.

The scheme was used by 15,800 people to contribute $4.165 billion in 2024–25, compared with 16,900 contributing $4.491 billion the previous year.

The wealth gap and transfer

As Australians retire with unprecedented levels of wealth, government spending on social safety nets for older Australians continues to grow.

Net tax and benefit changes for different age groups. Credit: Analysis by ANU Professor Robert Breunig

In 1971, just 17 per cent of Australians were over 55, while almost half the population was under 25. By 2028, these groups will be roughly even and by 2069 older people are projected to be the largest age group, and realestate.com.au senior economist Anne Flaherty says this is "going to be a big problem".

"Often the people who are you know living paycheck to paycheck are the ones who actually don't have access to a lot of the concessions that older Australians who who may be more cashed up have access to."

More reasons to stay

Another challenge is that the kinds of properties with the most capital growth are often larger houses, with more land in well-established suburbs, Flaherty said.

"So that's another incentive that people have not to leave their home, but to stay in that property and increase the capital gains they're going to see. (And) adult children can inherit that property, so it might be a way of keeping wealth in the family, which is inefficient because that home could have been used by someone who did need extra space."

Swapping stamp duty to a universal land tax is a "win-win for everyone over the long term", Flaherty said.

"The challenge, of course, is weaning state governments off stamp duty revenue over the short term is very difficult.

"This year is a good example of the problems with stamp duty, given the reduction in overall properties that have been selling. We're going to see a lot of state governments see their revenues take a big hit."

AHURI modelled the potential impact on house prices and rents of replacing stamp duty with a broad-based land tax, finding more affordable housing for both owner-occupiers and renters.

title: Australia's ruling on coal 'a clear signal' to the world, Pacific minister says
text:
In brief Tuvalu says a poorly attended climate summit still made an impact.

A landmark Australian ruling is being hailed beyond our shores.

Tuvalu's Climate Minister has hit back at claims that last week's Pre-COP event hosted by his country was a flop, while saying a phase-out of fossil fuels must be part of the discussion around COP31 in Türkiye.

Dr Maina Vakafua Talia also told SBS News his nation welcomed a landmark Australian High Court decision on coal and gas emissions, which provoked outcry from the mining sector, as a "clear signal" of moral responsibility.

Tuvalu, whose population numbers around 10,000, hosted a leader's gathering at last week's Pre-COP event shared with Fiji, part of a compromise struck by Australia to divide hosting rights with Türkiye.

The event came under heavy Australian media scrutiny, with shadow energy minister Dan Tehan labelling the event an "embarrassment" and a "flop" over the low number of leaders attending beyond a group from the Pacific.

While Talia acknowledged the Tuvalu meeting was only able to attract two global leaders from outside the Pacific (Timor-Leste and Mauritius), down from five initially expected, he described the turnout as "a big achievement for Tuvalu and for the Pacific."

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"We need to be very ambitious," he told SBS News in Canberra, talking up the event's shift from "a boring dialogue" to "a more moving, emotional engagement" focused on the challenges facing low-lying communities like his.

"The leaders were able to see for themselves, engage with the young ones, engage with our elders. One of the high representatives that came to Tuvalu told me, 'My heart bleeds when I saw the kids, when I saw our elders. Now I understand'."

The Taku Pakasoa Declaration agreed to at Pre-COP urged nations to act to keep the 1.5-degree climate target in reach, as well as increasing access to Climate Finance.

But there appears to be a diminishing appetite among nations for November's Antalya agreement to contain language focused on the phase-out of fossil fuels like Coal and Gas.

Türkiye's climate minister Murat Kurum, who will oversee the COP31 presidency, told the Guardian last week the world is "already in a transition" away from fossil fuels, reportedly suggesting the issue could be addressed indirectly through other means.

READ MORE The two-metre question that could wipe out a population

"If we are to discuss the 1.5 degrees, we are literally discussing the phasing out of fossil fuels," Talia said.

"We are talking about the backbone of some economies, but this is the reality that we have to face, and we really need to change the whole narrative, to change our priorities … to ensure that the survival of other peoples is always there."

Talia, who is set to share a related panel with energy minister Chris Bowen in Canberra, said he had faith Australia "can do more with the power that they have" to make the case for strong action, standing up to nations like India, Russia and China who are likely to argue for a moderate approach.

Climate ruling proof a moral responsibility

While leaders were gathering for Pre-COP, Australia's High Court delivered a landmark climate decision, finding in the case of Mount Pleasant Coal Mine in New South Wales, planning authorities must consider the entire carbon footprint of the project, including the emissions produced by the burning of fossil fuels overseas.

The decision referenced the 2025 International Court of Justice ruling brought on by Vanuatu, which found nations have international law obligations to protect the climate.

Talia said the Australian High Court ruling showed the impact of that ICJ precedent, and was one long-awaited by the Pacific nation.

"This is a good signal, a very clear signal, not just for the Pacific countries. It's really a moral responsibility for countries," he said.

The Australia-Tuvalu Falepili Union signed in 2024 was the first bilateral agreement to contain a significant pathway around climate mobility, with more than half the nation's population applying in the initial ballot.

"There is no treaty in this world we can allude to say that this is 100 per cent," Talia said, conceding "there are challenges, but they are manageable at the moment.

He said the risk of a brain drain was one his government would have to manage but rejected the claim the treaty was "creating an avenue for people to escape".

title: Is Australia prepared to cope with its 'modern-day success story'?
text:
IN BRIEF: Emergency departments will increasingly struggle to cope with an influx of elderly patients, a new report has found.

Experts say that older people are falling through the cracks at every level of the health and aged care systems.

Australians are living longer and the healthcare system is increasingly unable to cope, according to a new national report on the state of emergency departments (EDs).

The Australasian College of Emergency Medicine's (ACEM) third annual report notes that while Australia's ageing population is a "modern-day success story", the nation is not sufficiently prepared for the influx of elderly people into EDs.

From 2019 to 2024, the number of older people attending EDs increased by 16 per cent, compared with a 4 per cent increase among younger people, with half of all elderly presentations to an ED resulting in a hospital admission.

The group also found disparities in hospital care requirements between groups of older people.

While all non-Indigenous people aged 65 years and over were significantly more likely than younger people to be classified in higher urgency categories, arrive by ambulance and be admitted into hospital, that also holds for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people aged 50 years and over.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

ACEM president Dr Peter Allely said EDs were "far from ideal" environments to treat elderly patients, due to their "harsh lighting, loud noises and constant interruptions".

"We see too many frail people made afraid, confused and unwell by an unfamiliar environment, far away from their loved ones, familiar faces, supports and home comforts."

He said that, despite the "scale and predictability of demographic trends", governments across Australia had done little to prepare for the "volume and complexity of care needs" for the ageing population.

As a result, significant pressure was now being felt at "all levels" of the health system, including hospitals, primary and aged care facilities, and in-home support programs, he added.

ACEM is the organisation responsible for training emergency medicine specialists and setting standards for emergency care in Australia and New Zealand.

Across-the-board lack of preparedness

University of New South Wales professor in ageing health Lee-Fay Low agreed, saying she didn't think Australia had been doing anything long-term to prepare the health system for Australia's ageing population.

Similarly to Allely, Low said this lack of preparedness wasn't unique to hospitals, but could also be seen in primary care clinics, aged care facilities, and even among families.

Low, who is also leader of the Ageing and Health Research Group at the University of Sydney, said the ongoing aged care crisis was affecting people's ability to receive preventative care.

"Right now, because you have to wait for aged care, those things that might help might prevent you from going to emergency, like poor nutrition, ending up with an infection because your hygiene's not looked after."

READ MORE Aged care giant refunds $200,000 to residents over disputed living fees

Even since the Royal Commission into Aged Care handed down its final report in 2021, lengthy waitlists for aged care providers have seen many people go without crucial care, Low said.

"After the Aged Care Royal Commission, the government released more home care packages, allowing people to age in place without going into nursing homes. But that waitlist is a year long again now.

"The problem is that with the aged care reforms, things are worse now ... I mean, waiting a year is ridiculous.

"People living in their homes aren't really getting that aged care in a timely way, and that precedes these emergency visits."

READ MORE What 720 Australians reveal about ageing well — and the key to longevity

New health department data released yesterday found an average of 17 older Australians died while waiting to receive support at home care each day last year — an increase of more than a third on the previous year.

As of June 30, more than 106,000 Australians were on the official waiting list for a place in the Commonwealth-funded Support at Home program, while the ABC's Four Corners reported in August that the true number of people waiting was almost 154,000.

'Urgent action' needed

Older Australians made up only 17 per cent of the population in 2024 but accounted for almost a quarter of all ED presentations.

The ACEM report said that, without "urgent action", increased ED presentations by older people would disproportionately impact the healthcare system.

Using population growth modelling from the Australian Bureau of Statistics, the report projected a 177 per cent increase in total ED presentations between 2010 and 2050, noting projected increases of 242 per cent for people aged 65 to 84, and 411 per cent for people aged 85 and over.

ACEM is calling for federal, state and territory governments to urgently improve the quality of care older people receive across the health system, reduce ED demand, lift hospital capacity and provide sustainable hospital care for all Australians.

The government's latest Intergenerational Report projected rapid population ageing and falling fertility rates would fundamentally reshape the economy and budget out to 2065–66. By 2030, nearly one in five Australians will be aged 65 and over.

"The ratio of working people to older people is going to change substantively," Low said.

Allely warned that "Australia's health system and its health workforce are just not equipped for this demographic change."

More funding not the only remedy

Low said preparing for an ageing future required more than a funding boost.

"We always say we should have more funding, but I think where the funding is focused is important."

She also said proper reform would also require "an adjustment in presumptions and expectations Australians have for care as they get older".

"I think the presumption and the expectation in Australia is that when you get older, if you need care, you've paid taxes your whole life and the government will look after you. And that's already untrue, right? Aged care doesn't look after you straight away."

Low said a "national conversation" was needed to identify where the responsibility for care lies — whether it is with the government, or a co-contribution arrangement through which "as part of saving for retirement and super, that we also put aside some money, if we need help and we can pay for care".

Reforms also need to ensure the aged-care sector has a sufficient workforce, one-third of which is currently made up of migrants. Australia needs to reconsider decisions made around cutting migration, Low said.

She also suggested more families needed to start conversations about the "expectation that maybe mum and dad will need some help, and at that stage we might have to work less or chip in somehow to support the care".

But beyond families, she said, "this is not a conversation that we've had nationally".

title: Hackers hit French supermarket fridges, sparking fires and spoiling food
text:
In brief The refrigeration control systems of Danish manufacturer Danfoss were targeted in the attack.

The incident comes amid growing concern over potential havoc that can be caused in Europe by malicious cyberattacks.

Hackers raised the temperature of refrigerators and freezers at hundreds of French supermarkets to as high as 50C overnight, causing fires and spoiling food.

The Paris prosecutor's office said on Tuesday (AEDT) that a "large-scale" attack was "affecting connected refrigerators in several major food retailers across France", leading to food losses and fires.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has instructed France's National Cybersecurity Agency (ANSSI) to investigate, a spokesperson in his office said.

France was coordinating with European counterparts because other countries could also be affected, the person said, adding that authorities were assessing whether other French companies were at risk.

Félix Aimé, a senior cyber threat intelligence analyst at Sekoia Threat Detection and Research, said Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium had also been affected.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Carrefour said 80 of its supermarkets were hit, while Monoprix, which operates about 490 stores in France, said 5 per cent of its stores were affected.

Les Mousquetaires, owner of retailer Intermarché, said fridges at around 150 of its stores were heated up to 50C for six hours overnight. A spokesperson said staff discarded all affected food to eliminate health risks.

Paris resident Geert de Clercq witnessed staff at an Intermarché in central Paris throwing whole carts of defrosted frozen foods into a giant trash container, with molten ice cream sloshing out of broken tubs on the street.

READ MORE Why we're still living with password rules their creator regrets

Dominique Schelcher, the CEO of Coopérative U — a collective of independent hypermarkets and supermarkets — said his group had also been targeted.

"Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented," he wrote on X.

There was no immediate estimate of industry-wide losses, but Intermarché CEO Thierry Cotillard told BFM TV the "unprecedented" attack would represent losses amounting to "tens of millions of euros nationwide in a single day".

Christel Delberghe, director general at European retail association Eurocommerce, said: "This incident underlines the importance of resilience across the entire supply chain."

Cold aisles controlled via internet

Supermarket cold aisles are typically run by control panels that manage an entire store's fridges and freezers and can be accessed over the internet, which lets maintenance companies adjust them from anywhere.

The source close to Lecornu said ANSSI had identified a vulnerability in software supplied by Danish company Danfoss.

Danfoss said it was "aware of incidents in France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems".

The affected units "were running outdated firmware", Danfoss said, adding that it had "long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware and to migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions".

The attacks resemble disruptions reported at about a dozen US military commissaries in late August that led to food losses after fridges were affected.

Dutch retailer also reports 'cybersecurity incident'

Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize AD.AS, which operates the Netherlands' largest supermarket chain Albert Heijn and has major operations in the US, said it was dealing with a "security issue" on its network and had taken several systems offline as a precaution.

A message on the retailer's smartphone app said it was unable to deliver groceries because of a "cybersecurity incident".

Online orders account for about 10 per cent of Albert Heijn sales. Physical stores remained open, while Dutch news agency ANP reported that rival retailers had seen a surge in delivery orders.

Ahold Delhaize said there was no reason to see a link between the incidents in France and its supermarkets.

Ahold is the fourth-largest grocery retailer in the US. Websites for its Stop & Shop, Giant, Hannaford and Food Lion chains displayed notices saying "site temporarily down".

It was unclear whether other operations had been affected.

title: The surprising health condition some people develop after moving to Australia
text:
In brief Nearly one in four Australians experience hay fever, according to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare.

For some migrants, hay fever doesn't appear until years after they move to Australia.

Zoe had never experienced hay fever before moving to Australia.

But a few years after arriving, she began experiencing red and itchy eyes. At first, she assumed they were a reaction to her contact lenses.

When the symptoms worsened and returned year after year, she started looking for another explanation.

Along with itchy eyes, she said she developed severe nasal congestion and an urge to sneeze. After seeking medical advice, she was told she had hay fever.

"It took me years to realise," Zoe, who asked for her last name to be withheld for privacy reasons, told SBS Thai.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Allergic rhinitis, commonly known as hay fever, occurs when the immune system reacts to airborne allergens. Common triggers include pollen, dust mites, mould and animal dander (flakes of skin in fur, hair or feathers).

Nearly one in four Australians experience hay fever, according to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare.

For some migrants, the condition only emerges after several years of living in the country, with research suggesting exposure to new environmental allergens may play a role.

Why allergies can emerge years after migration

Dr Jason Yu, a Sydney-based general practitioner and clinical allergist, became interested in allergy medicine after moving between countries. He had not experienced allergies as a child but developed them years later.

He said allergies can develop at any stage of life, although they often first appear in childhood.

"We don't know the exact reasons why people develop allergies," Yu told SBS Thai.

One possible explanation for developing new allergies after migration is exposure to a novel environment, which can introduce people to allergens they hadn't previously encountered.

Yu said dust mite allergies are common in Sydney and other coastal areas, while grass pollen, including ryegrass pollen, was another prominent trigger in Australia.

"Pollen can be blown kilometres away," he said.

Pollen is a key trigger of hay fever. Source: AAP / Tracey Nearmy

Yu said there isn't yet a definitive explanation for why some people develop allergies and others don't.

Genetics and the development of the immune system may also play a role. Infections can also influence immune responses, although their relationship with allergy development is complex.

Research has previously documented the development of allergic conditions among people who migrate to Australia.

A 1996 study found up to 60 per cent of people who moved from South-East Asian countries to Australia developed hay fever, while 15 per cent developed asthma within their first 10 years in Australia.

A 2015 study from Curtin University also reported similar findings, suggesting people who migrated from China were more prone to allergies after moving to Australia.

For Hansa, whose last name has been withheld for privacy reasons, the first signs of hay fever were easy to mistake for a cold.

"One day, all of a sudden, my nose wouldn't stop running, my eyes were watering, and I kept sneezing," she told SBS Thai.

While living in Thailand, Hansa occasionally reacted to construction dust, but she hadn't experienced the same symptoms after moving to Australia.

About three years after her arrival, the symptoms began.

She had assumed that if she was allergic to something, the reaction would appear straight away, rather than emerge several years after the move.

Antihistamines are commonly used to manage hay fever, but Yu said the ideal form of treatment depends on a person's symptoms.

For those whose main symptom is nasal congestion, corticosteroid nasal sprays may be more effective than antihistamines alone, he said.

For persistent or more severe allergies, allergen immunotherapy may also be an option.

When hay fever becomes more serious

Hay fever and asthma are different but closely related conditions.

Hay fever primarily affects the eyes and upper airways, while asthma affects the lower airways and causes symptoms such as wheezing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath.

"If you feel short of breath, you feel like heaviness on your chest, you definitely should see someone about it," Yu said.

He said this was particularly important because, in rare circumstances, exposure to grass pollen can trigger a potentially life-threatening event known as thunderstorm asthma.

Asthma can cause severe breathing difficulties, raising the potential risks for undiagnosed persons. Source: AAP / Tracey Nearmy

Under certain weather conditions, storm outflows can concentrate grass pollen into smaller particles. When inhaled, those particles can penetrate deeper into the lungs, triggering inflammation and narrowing airways.

"It doesn't happen often, but if it does happen, it has really deadly consequences," Yu said.

Melbourne experienced what's considered the world's largest recorded epidemic of thunderstorm asthma in November 2016. Thousands of people developed breathing difficulties, placing significant pressure on the city's emergency services and hospitals.

The event also highlighted the disproportionate impact thunderstorm asthma can have on some migrant communities.

A study published by The Lancet in 2018 found people of Asian or Indian ethnicity were disproportionately impacted, representing 39 per cent of people who attended hospital. Six of the 10 who died were of South or Southeast Asian ethnicity.

Hay fever and asthma can also occur together, and Yu said some people may not realise they have both conditions.

"I've had a few patients come in; they didn't realise they had asthma as well; they thought they just had hay fever.

"But because I checked, I could actually identify they actually have asthma."

title: The country coming for a $20-billion Australian export market
text:
IN BRIEF: Brazil is the world's leading beef exporter and producer.

Commentators warn that shifts in global markets could see the country absorb Australia's markets.

Australian beef could face its toughest competition yet, as the world's leading producer encroaches on its traditional export markets.

Since the early 2000s, Brazil has consistently ranked as the world's leading beef producer, with an enormous 230 million-strong herd in 2024, more than the country's estimated population. The South American country is also the world's leading exporter, sending its beef to 130 different countries.

Australia has long prided itself on its beef exports: in 2025, 1.5 million tonnes of beef were sent to 83 countries. In 2025, the value of Australian beef exports was $19.6 billion, according to Australia's red meat research and marketing body, Meat and Livestock Australia (MLA).

But commentators are suggesting South American exporters are expanding in Australia's most important export markets — South Korea and Japan — which could have significant impacts on price competition over the coming months.

Speaking on a recent agribusiness podcast, Angus Gidley-Baird, senior animal proteins analyst at food and agribusiness bank Rabobank, said Australia’s beef sector should closely monitor developments in Brazil.

"Over the past few years, we’ve seen Brazil increase its presence in several of Australia’s export markets," Gidley-Baird said.

"Combined with changing trade dynamics involving China, the United States and Europe, it is becoming increasingly important for Australian producers and exporters to understand what is happening in the Brazilian beef sector."

Brazil already has a big presence in the Australian meat industry, through worldwide giant JBS. It's the biggest meat processing company in Australia, owning a series of foodlots and abattoirs, as well as the smallgoods company Primo Foods.

More than half of Brazil's beef exports are to China, and it hit its annual quota of 1.1 million tonnes for shipments to the country last month.

China's commerce ministry said it would start collecting an additional 55 per cent tariff on Brazil's beef shipments on 1 October after the South American country reached its annual ‌quota of 1.1 million tonnes.

Rabobank Brazil animal protein analyst Wagner Yanaguizawa said that new quota restrictions significantly reduced Brazilian shipments during the second half of 2025, creating surplus volumes that would need to be redirected elsewhere, and could translate into greater competition for Australia in alternative destination markets.

Australia exported beef to 83 countries in 2025. Source: Getty / Darren Hunt / FlickrVision

Yanaguizawa said the United States was likely to absorb some of the displaced volume, while the Middle East, Indonesia, Vietnam, Chile and the United Kingdom also presented opportunities. Those markets would not be sufficient to offset reduced Chinese demand, though, he said.

Yanaguizawa said the potential opening of Japan and South Korea to Brazilian beef also warrants close attention from Australian industry participants.

"Japanese and South Korean inspections of Brazilian processing plants had been completed, and final reports were pending before market access decisions could be finalised. Industry expectations are that access could be granted later this year," Yanaguizawa said.

"These two markets are very important for Australia, and soon Australia may have a new competitor," he said.

The MLA is aware of the shift. On an August 2026 podcast, the corporation's regional manager for Southeast Asia, Valeska, said that as global trade patterns shifted, Australian beef volumes had been redirected from China into Southeast Asia.

At the same time, competition across Southeast Asia was intensifying, as exporters from South America actively pursued new opportunities across the region.

"The South Americans are really active and quite aggressive. At the [World Food Expo in the Philippines] yesterday, we spoke with Brazilian packers who indicated they're looking at alternative markets."

Valeska said she believed Australia's long-term investment in Southeast Asia positioned the industry well.

"We're not resting on our laurels. Australian beef is definitely ramping up activities across Southeast Asia, and I think it's an opportunity to really secure the premium segment while continuing to grow demand through other channels."

title: Josh Frydenberg says 'things have to change' as he questions Liberal leadership
text:
In brief Former federal treasurer Josh Frydenberg has criticised Angus Taylor's leadership of the Liberal Party.

He told Nine's 60 Minutes that 'things have to change' after Liberal polling fell to an all-time low.

Angus Taylor would welcome the political return of Josh Frydenberg to parliament, despite the former treasurer attacking his leadership of the Liberal Party.

Frydenberg used an interview to criticise Taylor's handling of the party, saying the current leader had contributed to Liberal polling being at an "all-time low".

"Things have to change, because there's something existential about the threat that I think the party now faces," he told Nine's 60 Minutes on Sunday night.

"[Taylor is] getting [criticism] from lots of corners. People are saying that the Liberal Party needs to do better."

The latest Newspoll had the Coalition's primary support at 20 per cent, compared to Labor's 29 per cent and One Nation's 26 per cent.

Excerpts from Frydenberg's memoir, which is likely to contain policy suggestions, have fuelled rumours that he is planning to make a political comeback.

"Look, I certainly haven't closed the door, but I don't need to rush to a decision. The next election is 18 months away," he said.

Despite the criticism, Taylor said his former Liberal colleague would be welcomed back into the fold should he decide to run.

The Liberal Party's fortunes have not improved after Angus Taylor took over as leader in February. Source: AAP / Bianca de Marchi

"I welcome every Liberal who cares about the future of our nation — and I know Josh does — to put shoulder to the wheel in the coming months to get rid of a rotten Labor government and make the change that Australia needs happen," he told reporters in Canberra on Monday.

"I ask all Liberals and Nationals and people who are supportive of our view about where the country needs to go … to get in there and help in any way they can."

Frydenberg held the Melbourne seat of Kooyong for 12 years from 2010 and was treasurer in the Morrison government, including through the COVID-19 pandemic.

He lost the seat to independent MP Monique Ryan at the 2022 election, in which she won almost 53 per cent of the two-party preferred vote.

Ryan appeared unfazed by her competition's possible return.

"I'm not bothered either way," she told Nine's Today program.

"Josh does have a track record with the Kooyong community."

"He was the member for that seat for 12 years, and in 2022, our community rejected him because they were so frustrated with his inability to affect any change to government policy on climate change.

"People were unhappy with his economic management."

Opposition treasury spokesperson Tim Wilson has encouraged others to put themselves forward as Liberal candidates. Source: AAP / Mick Tsikas

Opposition treasury spokesperson Tim Wilson encouraged people to "put themselves forward" as candidates to create a stronger Liberal Party.

"I encourage them to do so, so they can be part of a winning team. So we can have an Angus Taylor-led government," he told ABC Radio.

"What we need is people who've got courage in their hearts and are prepared to make the sacrifices necessary for public office."

An eight-year-old girl’s death was preventable, a coroner has found as she criticised a Melbourne emergency department doctor’s response. Amrita Varshini Lanka’s parents nodded and wiped away tears as Victoria’s deputy state coroner Paresa Spanos handed down her findings on Wednesday. Chandra Sekhar Lanka and Satya Tarapureddi arrive at an inquest into the death of their daughter Amrita Lanka. AAP Amrita died from lymphocytic myocarditis, or inflammation of the heart muscle, at Monash Children’s Hospital on April 30, 2022. She had presented at the emergency department about 1pm on April 29, following two days of stomach pain, nausea and vomiting.

Advertisement

Related Article Coroners Court of Victoria Hospital ignored repeated pleas for help before eight-year-old’s death, court told Testing quickly ruled out appendicitis, so hospital staff began working on the basis she had gastroenteritis. Early the next morning, Amrita’s mother Satya Tarapureddi raised concerns with staff that her daughter was experiencing chest pain and a shortness of breath. Amrita underwent an electrocardiogram (ECG) half an hour later at 3.30am, which came back abnormal and led the emergency department registrar Patrick Tan to suspect she had myocarditis. He consulted with another colleague, who agreed with his preliminary diagnosis.

Advertisement

But neither doctor seemed to appreciate the severity of Amrita’s condition, the coroner said. Amrita’s blood pressure was not measured at that time, but other testing showed elevated lactate, which signified that she was deteriorating. Amrita Lanka died in hospital aged eight. Justin McManus Despite this, Dr Tan determined that Amrita did not look unwell. He did not attend to the eight-year-old again until 5.30am, when it was clear her condition had worsened. Her care was escalated to senior clinicians and specialist units, but she suffered a brief cardiac arrest at 7.30am.

Advertisement

Staff then organised emergency transfer to the Royal Children’s Hospital and a crew arrived about 8.51am, by which time Amrita had gone into prolonged cardiac arrest. Despite efforts at CPR, she could not be saved. In a 2024 inquest into Amrita’s death, Monash Health admitted staff had failed to appreciate the seriousness of the girl’s condition. Amrita’s family says that if tests had been interpreted correctly sooner, her case would have been escalated to an on-call cardiologist. Justin McManus On Wednesday, Spanos determined Amrita’s death was preventable. “When the ECG had been completed and the elevated lactate was available [at about 4am], Amrita’s life could have been saved,” the coroner said in her findings.

Advertisement

“While I accept that [emergency departments] are busy places and Dr Tan was a relatively junior doctor with many responsibilities, the clinical management and care he provided to Amrita was wanting,” the coroner said. His actions, Spanos told the court, “thereby caused or contributed to her death”. The coroner did not make any formal recommendations, instead commending Monash Health for undertaking an internal review following Amrita’s death. Spanos acknowledged the hospital had implemented a series of changes as a result, including requiring emergency department clinicians to notify on-call consultants in specific cases. The coroner, who at times appeared to hold back tears while reading her findings, offered her condolences to Amrita’s parents seated in the courtroom.

Moonlight Resources has put some serious numbers on the table at its Clermont gold project in central Queensland, defining a significant new exploration target of up to 662,000 ounces of near-surface gold. The study has prompted the company to launch a 13,000-metre reverse circulation (RC) drilling program to test its ambitious new objective. The exploration target covers three key prospects – Leo Grande, Goldfinger and Petersens. It ranges between 16.2 and 19.8 million tonnes at grades of between 0.94 and 1.15 grams per tonne (g/t) gold, totalling 443,000 to 662,000 ounces of the yellow metal. The company has emphasised that the exploration target is conceptual in nature and at this stage, requires more work to determine whether a gold resource can be identified and quantified in potentially economic terms. Moonlight Resources’ phase two reverse circulation drilling underway at its Leo Grande prospect, part of the company’s Clermont Project in Central Queensland. The lion’s share of the target relates to the central Leo Grande prospect, which contributes between 281,000 and 420,000 ounces of gold. The Goldfinger and Petersens prospects add some higher-grade spice, with the southern Goldfinger prospect tipped to potentially contain between 95,000 and 142,000 ounces at a solid 1.2 to 1.5g/t gold. The more northerly Petersons prospect offers the remaining potential - 67,000 to 100,000 ounces of gold at 1g/t to 1.22g/t. Moonlight’s 13,000m RC drilling campaign is now underway, with the drill bit already probing Goldfinger’s potential. The program will drill an estimated 5000m into the prospect, with a further 4000m allocated to Petersens and Leo Grande.

Advertisement

‘We believe Clermont can develop into a significant gold project.’ Moonlight Resources managing director Greg Starr The Clermont project is centred 15 kilometres west of the historic Clermont township, in a hotspot with a strong history of gold mining, producing roughly 400,000 ounces since 1878. The greater region is richly endowed and hosts several multi-million-ounce gold deposits, providing a compelling case for the region’s prospectivity. Two notable nearby projects within the Drummond Basin - the extensive regional-scale geological complex that hosts Moonlight’s Clermont ground - include GBM Resources’ one-million-ounce Twin Hills gold resource north of Clermont and its 330,000-ounce Mount Coolon gold project northwest of Emerald and north of Clermont. The Drummond Basin overall is a premier gold province credited with a total historical production and known endowment of up to 7.5 million ounces of gold. Moonlight’s exploration model rests on a solid foundation of historical work combined with its own recent successes. Earlier drilling by the company of an estimated 15,000m at Leo Grande returned a swag of broad, near-surface gold hits, including a notable 42m at 1.01g/t gold from surface and 40m at 1.31g/t gold from 76m. Moonlight Resources managing director Greg Starr said: “This Exploration Target puts some significant numbers around exactly what excites us about Clermont – the combination of potential scale, gold mineralisation relatively close to surface and the opportunity to test extensions that remain open. We’ve brought together the historical and recent drilling information at Leo Grande, Goldfinger and Petersens, which gives us a much clearer picture of the potential opportunity and where we intend to focus our efforts.”

While gold is Moonlight’s primary focus, its Clermont tenure also hosts the Peak Downs copper prospect, a few kilometres south of Clermont, which the company describes as a “high-grade copper sleeper opportunity”. This is hardly surprising, given that the prospect was historically mined between 1862 and 1877, reportedly producing around 100,000 tonnes of ore at an eye-watering average grade estimated at 17 per cent copper. Management is targeting near-term delivery of a maiden gold resource estimate for the Clermont gold project, which will initially incorporate its Leo Grande and Goldfinger deposits. Moonlight also says that it expects to deliver a much-anticipated initial copper resource estimate for the Peak Downs project before the end of the year. With a significant exploration target now up in lights on the board, Moonlight’s focus has shifted to the drill bit and with a hefty 13,000m drilling campaign already in full swing, the market may not have to wait long to find out if this geological model in a highly prospective region can be converted into real gold ounces. Test cricket great Steve Waugh is calling on Australia’s selectors to stop “messing around” and “pick and stick” at the top of the batting order. That includes keeping first Test hero Matt Renshaw, who made 190 and 82 in Durban to set up Australia’s 214-run win in the three-match series, in the middle order. Matt Renshaw celebrates his fighting century. Getty Images “They need a consistent line-up,” Waugh said. After suffering an embarrassing nine-wicket loss to Bangladesh in August to kick-start Australia’s marathon 12 months of cricket, Pat Cummins’ men continued their resurgence on Tuesday by taking down the world Test champions in Durban.

Advertisement

The outstanding victory came despite some day one wobbles, where the visitors slumped to 6-124 before Renshaw batted superbly with the tail to register his second Test century – and first in almost a decade – to set up the win. The 30-year-old faced 397 deliveries during his 190. Despite several teammates getting starts in the second innings, including Nic Maddinson (48), Marnus Labuschagne (37) and Beau Webster (39 not out), the big Queenslander was again the only Australian to pass 50. Loading Following the Test, Cummins said Australia’s brains trust, including coach Andrew McDonald and selectors, would continue to be flexible with the top seven. That included the possibility of Renshaw moving up to the top of the order and either Travis Head or Maddinson sliding down to No.5. “We’re always big on how the order functions as a whole,” Cummins said. “Seeing the way that he played spin in the one-day series led me to the thought [that] he would look pretty good at No.5.

Advertisement

“Give us a few days, we’ll look at the conditions of the next Test and whether that’s still the case. I mean, it’s got to be pretty compelling to move him from there. But we’ve seen Travis Head down at No.5 as well — [he] can do a job.” Cummins added: “I think bringing Maddo in, we really like the idea of bringing that flexibility. That unlocks a lot – Trav back to No.5, Renners down at No.5, even Maddo himself at No.5. We haven’t had that option the last few years where we feel like we’ve got plenty of options at the top. You know we’re very big on that flexibility.” Matt Renshaw and Pat Cummins celebrate on day five in Durban. AP But Waugh said the time for tinkering was over, especially given there were crunch series – five Tests in India and an Ashes in England – in the next 12 months. “We’ve been messing around with the top order for the last couple of years and it hasn’t worked, so they’ve got to pick and stick now,” he said.

Advertisement

Having earned the reputation as Australia’s “Ice Man” during his illustrious career, Waugh said he was particularly impressed by Renshaw’s application in Durban. “It was an outstanding win,” Waugh said. “And great to see some old-fashioned Test match batting from Renshaw. I think he led the way – the old values of shot selection and patience and determination – and it was great to see some Test match batting like that. It was fantastic. “I think the other guys will follow the way he batted. I think it’s a great role model for not only our team, but for world cricket – how to be successful in Test matches.” Asked whether Renshaw should stay in the middle order – where Waugh made his name during a 168-Test career that produced 10,927 runs at an average of 51.06 – the former captain said he would not change a winning formula. “It’s obviously a career-defining moment for him and could be the catalyst for great things going forward,” Waugh said. “Don’t mess around with that now. He’s been successful, and he’s comfortable, so I’d keep him there for sure.” As for Maddinson, whose 38-ball 48 got Australia off to a flyer in the second innings following his painful 33-ball first-innings duck, Waugh admitted it was a “left-field selection” to recall the 34-year-old, but hoped he continued to build a case for selection. “I wanted to see him get runs. He’s in the team now. Let’s hope he can get some runs,” Waugh said. The second Test starts on Sunday at St George’s Park, Gqeberha.

PLC Resources has taken to the skies, metaphorically speaking, to launch a two-stage satellite geo-spectral survey across its Abbotts gold project in Western Australia’s Murchison region, to pinpoint alteration zones and structures, sharpening the gold target discovery process. The company says its survey will cover all four of its Abbotts tenements spanning 205 square kilometres and will sift through PLC’s ground for large mineral alteration and undetected structures that can be tell-tale signs of orogenic gold mineralisation. Hyperspectral imagery over PLC Resources’ Abbotts gold project in WA will be harnessed to define structural gold targets for maiden discovery. The first stage involves a regional screening using hyperspectral EnMAP imagery by remote-sensing specialists Geo Spectra. Multispectral data will then map the alteration geological structures in greater detail across the entire project and over an additional 300 square kilometres of surrounding ground. The second, higher-resolution stage will allow Geo Spectra to zoom in on priority areas with imagery as sharp as 31 centimetres, mapping telltale iron oxides, clays and sulphates to refine targets for a boots-on-the-ground follow-up.

Advertisement

‘Hyperspectral and high-resolution satellite data can help map alteration minerals and fine-scale structures.’ PLC Resources executive director Simon Phillips The satellite survey builds on PLC’s recent high-resolution airborne magnetic survey, which revealed a large-scale fold structure considered highly prospective for gold deposition. Management says the structure is a crustal-level feature that extends for more than 14km of strike and, importantly, continues south into ground held by recent WA discovery dynamo New Murchison Gold. New Murchison has been making waves in the region, successfully trucking its high-grade gold discoveries to nearby toll-treating facilities, providing a compelling real-world example of the Abbotts greenstone’s unloved potential. PLC Resources executive director Simon Phillips said: “This survey gives us a project-wide view of Abbotts that we can’t get from the ground alone. Hyperspectral and high-resolution satellite data can help map alteration minerals and fine-scale structures that may be associated with gold mineralisation, across all four of our tenements at once.” The company’s move comes as exploration activity continues to ramp up across the white-hot Murchison, with nearby explorers committing to significant exploration programs in hopes of becoming the next New Murchison Gold story - recently capped at $950 million.

Advertisement

King River Resources recently launched a massive 11,000-metre drilling campaign at its Mindoolah gold project, while new players such as Parbo Resources, Golden Dragon and Reach Resources have all expanded their footprint in the region. The company recently completed a follow-up reverse circulation drilling program at its Rochefort gold prospect within Abbotts, with assay results currently pending. Geological logging from that campaign confirmed the target host rock had been intersected, with multiple accounts of potential gold-bearing sulphide alterations. The real test, however, will come when the assays land, potentially revealing a virgin gold discovery. PLC says, beyond drilling a Rochefort, it expects a prioritised target map from the new satellite survey within four to six weeks. The results will be integrated with recent magnetic survey data to rank targets for follow-up field exploration and aircore drilling. With New Murchison recently stacking up multiple high-grade discoveries next door along what appears to be a highly prospective, unloved gold belt, the company has plenty of reason to feel ambitious about its unfolding gold story at Abbotts. Its high-tech targeting could fast-track the hunt for a discovery of its own, with the coming months shaping up as a potentially pivotal period for the Perth-based explorer. NSW Premier Chris Minns has emerged victorious in a stoush over a controversial Central West gold mine after the Federal Court threw out a ban made by then-environment minister Tanya Plibersek, who stalled the mine on Indigenous heritage grounds. Federal Court Justice James Stellios on Wednesday decided to send the $1.3 billion McPhillamys mine proposal back to the current minister Murray Watt, determining Plibersek’s original decision lacked procedural fairness. The proposed McPhillamys gold mine would process as much as 8.5 million tonnes of ore a year. Nick Moir The decision did not make any judgment about the merits of any claims of Indigenous heritage in the area, but found Plibersek’s decision-making was flawed. That declaration prevented Regis Resources from building a tailings dam to store byproducts from mining operations at the headwaters of the Belubula River, after an Indigenous group argued the area was significant to a Dreaming story about the blue banded bee. The mining company argued that made the project unfeasible.

Advertisement

The declaration also triggered unrest between the state and federal governments, with Premier Chris Minns insisting the mine must go ahead. The state government had originally approved the project. Related Article Climate policy ‘Triply nervous’: Massive coal mine braced for challenge after High Court ruling “I want that mine to go ahead, I understand that that’s not the view of the federal government, but we need the investment,” Minns said before the judgment on Wednesday. “There are more people in mining jobs in NSW today than there were when we were elected in March of 2023. We’re proud of that.” When asked if the then-environment minister had made the wrong call when she made the order blocking the mine, Minns replied: “Yes”.

Advertisement

Plibersek’s statement of reasons for the declaration said she “could not be assured that the NSW legislative framework as it currently stands can adequately protect the specified area”. Watt said in a statement the federal government respects the court’s decision and is getting advice on next steps. He said the court’s findings highlighted the complexities of the current cultural heritage processes. “First Nations people, industry and state and territory governments have been clear with us for some time that they feel the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Heritage Protection (ATSIHP) Act doesn’t give enough certainty. We remain committed to working alongside them on a better system,” he said. NSW Resources Minister Courtney Houssos said the mine had already gone through a “robust” planning process and said critical minerals projects were important to diversify the state’s economy. “Protecting Aboriginal cultural heritage and progressing key mining projects should not be a zero-sum proposition,” she said.

Advertisement

After making the declaration in 2024, Plibersek rejected suggestions from Regis Resources that the ban killed the project, insisting the mine could still go ahead if the dam was moved. The company said finding a new site for approval would take up to 10 years, but the state government flagged it would fast-track the project. The application to protect the dam area was made by Wiradjuri-Gamillaroi woman Nyree Reynolds on behalf of the Wiradyuri Traditional Owners Central West Aboriginal Corporation. Minns told a budget estimates hearing in 2024 that the local Aboriginal Land Council had been consulted as part of the original approval process. In a statement to the ASX from Regis Resources CEO Jim Beyer after the judgment, Beyer said the company would actively participate in any redetermination of the Indigenous heritage claim by the current minister. “After considerable delay and uncertainty, and more than two years of time lost, we are eager to move forward. We look forward to engaging constructively with the Department through the redetermination process, and to advance one of Australia’s largest undeveloped gold projects – one with the potential to deliver lasting economic and social benefits to the Central NSW region and our broader stakeholder community,” he said. title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years

Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.

"I wouldn't usually ever buy more than one ticket a day, but when I realised I'd only bought the Slikpik, I thought I'd pop back because I like playing the same numbers.

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.
